## Impact
This is the [code assessment of the EIP-4788 contract](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/65d35b01a4034b72499019e8/664203f92deb52f6d21723cb_ChainSecurity_Ethereum_Foundation_EIP-4788_Contract_Audit_compressed.pdf)
Quoting 8.1.2 Integration Guidelines for Developers:
> The calldata has to be __exactly 32 bytes__ and should only contain the timestamp, in big-endian format, which is the EVM default.

However, `NativeVault::_getParentBlockRoot` uses `bytes` as calldata for the staticall to `Constants.BEACON_ROOTS_ADDRESS` because `abi.encode` returns `bytes` not `bytes32`, NOT EXACTLY 32 BYTES. This could cause failures in retrieving parent block roots, which are critical for various operations in the `NativeVault` contract, e.g., snapshot creation and validating withdrawal credentials.

```js
function _getParentBlockRoot(uint64 timestamp) internal view returns (bytes32) {
    //@audit `abi.encode` returns bytes not bytes32!!!
    (bool success, bytes memory result) = Constants.BEACON_ROOTS_ADDRESS.staticcall(abi.encode(timestamp)); 
    ...
}
```

There is a number of other non-compliance instances too, including:
> 8.1.3 . Due to the points above, smart contract developers might perform a low-level call in the respective smart contract language. That low-level call generally does not perform checks, such as sufficient return data. Hence, smart contracts performing such a low-level call should check that the RETURNDATASIZE == 32 using the features of the respective language.

However in the code, result is directly casted to `bytes32` without prior check of `RETURNDATASIZE`:
```js
...
if (success && result.length > 0) {
    return abi.decode(result, (bytes32));
} else {
    revert BeaconRootFetchError();
}
...
```
 
## Tools Used
- Manual review.
- EIP 4877 integration guidelines.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Refactor code to comply with integration guidelines.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Core.sol#L233-L243


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`Core::requestSlashing` allows a slashing to be requested for a given operator+vault by a DSS. A queued slashing is returned. Anyone can then call `Core::finalizeSlashing` to effectively slash funds from the corresponding operator and by consequence slash users depositing to his vault. Interestingly, there's this check in `finalizeSlashing`:
```js
if (queuedSlashing.timestamp + Constants.SLASHING_VETO_WINDOW > block.timestamp) {
    revert MinSlashingDelayNotPassed();
}
```
So there's this `Constants.SLASHING_VETO_WINDOW` where an entity called `SLASHING VETO COMMITTEE`, a trusted role that can overturn/cancel a slashing for any reason by calling `Core::cancelSlashing` during the corresponding `SLASHING_VETO_WINDOW`. Any attempt to finalize slashing during that window will revert.
Now a possible scenario is that `requestSlashing` is called on an operator, then for some reason the vault is paused by owner some time before the end of `SLASHING_VETO_WINDOW`, and unpaused after the veto window expired therefore any right to benefit from veto is lost as well. We emphisize that the veto committee can't call `cancelSlashing` because it's paused. If the operator was wrongly requested to be slashed i.e, the veto was going to be in his favor and cancel the slashing, anyone can then call `finalizeSlashing`, the earlier check for veto window expiry above will pass and the operator and user funds that must have been not slashed will be slashed and lost!!!

To summarize:
1. DSS initiates slashing via `requestSlashing`
2. Owner pauses `cancelSlashing` among other or all functionalities before `SLASHING_VETO_WINDOW` expiration.
3. `SLASHING_VETO_WINDOW` expires during pause.
4. Owner unpauses the system.
5. Anyone can now execute `finalizeSlashing`, causing loss of funds to users.

The impact is High (loss of user funds), the likelihood is Low (only when functions are paused).

## Tools Used
Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
There is more than 1 solution to consider:
- Remove pausability from `cancelSlashing`.
- If not, allow for a `PAUSING_COOLDOWN_WINDOW` to finish stuck issues during pausing like exercising veto on wrong slashing requests.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/Vault.sol#L110-L119


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Loss of assets for the affected users.

## Proof of Concept
During minting, the user deposits the underlying asset into the `Vault` contract, and the `Vault` contract uses the
`deposit/mint` function to mint shares to the user.

Vault.sol#deposit():
```solidity
    function deposit(uint256 assets, address to, uint256 minSharesOut)
        external
        nonReentrant
        whenFunctionNotPaused(Constants.PAUSE_VAULT_DEPOSIT_SLIPPAGE)
        returns (uint256 shares)
    {
        if (assets == 0) revert ZeroAmount();
        shares = super.deposit(assets, to);
        if (shares < minSharesOut) revert NotEnoughShares();
    }
```

Vault.sol#mint():
```solidity
    function mint(uint256 shares, address to)
        public
        override(ERC4626, IVault)
        whenFunctionNotPaused(Constants.PAUSE_VAULT_MINT)
        nonReentrant
        returns (uint256 assets)
    {
        if (shares == 0) revert ZeroShares();
        assets = super.mint(shares, to);
    }
```
These functions use the standard functions of ERC4626, so the number of shares minted depends on the current size of the `Vault` (i.e. `totalAssets() and `totalSupply()`).

The current size of the `Vault` can increase or decrease at any time depending on the current on-chain conditions when the transaction is executed.
As a result, the current size can change due to malicious actions of an attacker (donate attack) or phenomena such as rounding in large transactions.
if the current size changes, the number of shares minted will change (more or less than expected).

As you can see in the provided code snippet, the `deposit()` function applies slippage control to prevent any malicious frontrunning, but the `mint()` function does not apply slippage control.

Assuming that Alice decides to deposit x USDC and mint 100 shares off-chain.
When she executes the TX, the size increases and the amount of the underlying token that she is going to deposit can become bigger than expected amount. The slippage is greater than she can accept.

In summary, the `mint` function lacks the slippage control that allows the users to revert if the amount of the underlying token they deposits is bigger than the amount they expected.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Implement a slippage control that allows the users to revert if the amount of the underlying token they deposits is bigger than the amount they expected.


## Assessed type

MEV

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/a9658bccc884eb72538875c3940c6b507e06d4ca/src/entities/Operator.sol#L126


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `finishUpdateStakeHook()` selector from the `IDSS` interface, indicates that the incoming address parameter is supposed to be the `operator` address. However, the `Core::finalizeUpdateVaultStakeInDSS()` function can be called by any user. Because of this `msg.sender` is propagated to `Operator::validateAndUpdateVaultStakeInDSS()`, where it is finally sent as an `operator` parameter to `finishUpdateStakeHook()` in `abi.encodeWithSelector(dss.finishUpdateStakeHook.selector, msg.sender)`. Because of this, any arbitrary user will be treated as an operator which allows malicious users to execute the associated logic, which could involve something like registering the address to receive rewards.

This issue was reported in a previous [audit](https://code4rena.com/reports/2024-06-karak-pro-league) of Karak, made by Code4Arena. Both the auditing team and the protocol have confirmed that it should be fixed, however, it appears to be still valid.

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/interfaces/IDSS.sol#L15
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Core.sol#L146
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/Operator.sol#L126

1. An operator initiates `requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS()`, which goes through successfully and emits the updated stake information -> `emit RequestedStakeUpdate(updatedStake)`
2. Alice intercepts this emission and then calls `finalizeUpdateVaultStakeInDSS()` with the operator's `queuedStake`. This in turn will send Alice's address as an operator's address in the `finishUpdateStakeHook()` function, incorrectly allowing her to do malicious actions to the protocol.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

If `Core::requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS()` is meant to be callable by anyone, then change which address is being sent in the `HookLib.callHookIfInterfaceImplemented()` function in `Operator::validateAndUpdateVaultStakeInDSS()` from `msg.sender` to `queuedStakeUpdate.operator`

```diff
diff --git a/src/entities/Operator.sol b/src/entities/Operator.sol
index 31a3964..7425cf1 100644
--- a/src/entities/Operator.sol
+++ b/src/entities/Operator.sol
@@ -123,7 +123,7 @@ library Operator {
         IDSS dss = queuedStakeUpdate.updateRequest.dss;
         HookLib.callHookIfInterfaceImplemented({
             dss: dss,
-            data: abi.encodeWithSelector(dss.finishUpdateStakeHook.selector, msg.sender),
+            data: abi.encodeWithSelector(dss.finishUpdateStakeHook.selector, queuedStakeUpdate.operator),
             interfaceId: dss.finishUpdateStakeHook.selector,
             ignoreFailure: true,
             hookCallGasLimit: self.hookCallGasLimit,
```





## Assessed type

Access Control

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Using `isSmartContract()` to distinguish between Externally Owned Accounts (EOAs) and contracts in Ethereum is no longer reliable due to proxy contracts and contract creation during transaction execution. This method may inaccurately classify contracts as EOAs or vice versa, especially post-transaction. 

## Proof of Concept
 
When a Distributed Secure Service (DSS) is being registered in the `Core.sol` contract, it does the following check:

> if (!self.isVaultImplAllowlisted(newVaultImpl)) revert VaultImplNotAllowlisted();

However, this check can be false-positive:


* Function is called in the constructor. Address.isContract() checks for the code length, but during construction code length is 0.

* A smart contract that has not been deployed yet can be used. The CREATE2 opcode can be used to deterministically calculate the address of a smart contract before it is created. This means that the user can bypass this check by calling this function before deploying the contract.


## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

It is generally not recommended to enforce an address to be only EOA or vice-versa and AFAIK, this is impossible to implement due to the aforementioned cases. I recommend the protocol team take a closer look at this and build the protocol with the assumption that `address(dss) != EOA`. OpenZeppelin's Address library deprecated `isContract()` (which uses the same logic) recognizing these limitations.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/Core.sol#L146-L153


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details

`Core::requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS()` allows only operators that are registered to a certain DSS to stake/unstake vaults to it. However this can be bypassed because `Core::finalizeUpdateVaultStakeInDSS()` doesn't check if the operator is still registered to the certain DSS, thus an operator can unregister from the DSS between the requested update and the finalization. Let's see how this is a problem:

1. An operator is registered to a certain DSS and calls `Core::requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` to stake a vault.
2. Now there is a 9 days delay until someone can execute the finalization of the update.
3. The operator calls `Core::unregisterOperatorFromDSS()`. Since the state is not updated from the requested vault update and the operator still doesn't have any vaults staked to the DSS, the transaction executes successfully and now the operator is no longer staked to the DSS.
4. The rest of `MIN_STAKE_UPDATE_DELAY` passes and now either the operator or a random person calls `Core::finalizeUpdateVaultStakeInDSS()` to stake the vault to the DSS. Since a check is missing here to make sure that the operator is still registered to the DSS, the transaction executes, the state is updated and now this vault is staked to the DSS.
5. Now the above-mentioned vault cannot be unstaked, because in the `Core::requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` there is a check if the operator is registered to the DSS, but he is not. The DSS cannot request slashing because there is a check to see if the operator is registered to the DSS, this means that  the operator can do whatever he wants and still be left unpunished by the DSS. `Core::operatorState[operator].vaultStakedInDssMap[dss]` will contain the inaccessible vault.

## Impact

Does an incorrect state update to the `vaultStakedInDssMap` mapping which could lead to a lot of problems including unfair distribution of rewards, inability of slashing.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

In `Operator::validateAndUpdateVaultStakeInDSS()` check if the operator is still registered to the DSS.

```diff
function validateAndUpdateVaultStakeInDSS(CoreLib.Storage storage self, QueuedStakeUpdate memory queuedStakeUpdate)
        external
    {
        State storage operatorState = self.operatorState[queuedStakeUpdate.operator];
+       checkIfOperatorIsRegInRegDSS(self, queuedStakeUpdate.operator, queuedStakeUpdate.updateRequest.dss);
        validateQueuedStakeUpdate(operatorState, queuedStakeUpdate);
        updateVaultStakeInDSS(
            operatorState,
            queuedStakeUpdate.updateRequest.vault,
            queuedStakeUpdate.updateRequest.dss,
            queuedStakeUpdate.updateRequest.toStake
        );
        delete operatorState.pendingStakeUpdates[queuedStakeUpdate.updateRequest.vault];
        IDSS dss = queuedStakeUpdate.updateRequest.dss;
        HookLib.callHookIfInterfaceImplemented({
            dss: dss,
            data: abi.encodeWithSelector(dss.finishUpdateStakeHook.selector, msg.sender),
            interfaceId: dss.finishUpdateStakeHook.selector,
            ignoreFailure: true,
            hookCallGasLimit: self.hookCallGasLimit,
            supportsInterfaceGasLimit: self.supportsInterfaceGasLimit,
            hookGasBuffer: self.hookGasBuffer
        });
    }
```


## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/entities/Operator.sol#L128


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In `Operator::validateAndUpdateVaultStakeInDSS()` `ignoreFailure` is set to true which means the DSS cannot cancel a started update even if the vault doesn't meet its conditions anymore.

```solidity
HookLib.callHookIfInterfaceImplemented({
            dss: dss,
            data: abi.encodeWithSelector(dss.finishUpdateStakeHook.selector, msg.sender),
            interfaceId: dss.finishUpdateStakeHook.selector,
@->         ignoreFailure: true,
            hookCallGasLimit: self.hookCallGasLimit,
            supportsInterfaceGasLimit: self.supportsInterfaceGasLimit,
            hookGasBuffer: self.hookGasBuffer
        });
```

## Proof of Concept

Let's look at the following example:

1. A vault is staked to one DSS.
2. Now the operator wants to stake the same vault to another DSS, but that DSS has a condition for accepting new vaults (for example it requires the TVL of the vault to be >= 100 000e18 tokens, assuming 18 decimal precision). The vault currently meets that requirement so the operator calls `Core::requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS()` to stake that vault. The DSS accepts it (doesn't revert).
3. There is a 9 days delay until the update can be finalized. That is a lot of time and in that time a lot can happen. For example the first DSS can execute a slashing (it takes 2 days for the slashing to finalize which is way less than the delay of the update) and now `totalAssets()` of the vault are <= 100 000e18 which no longer meets the second DSS requirement.
4. The operator executes `Core::finalizeUpdateVaultStakeInDSS()` and even if the DSS reverts, it will not affect the transcation and the state will be updated, so now that vault is staked in both DSSs without the consent of the second one.

Notice that `Core::requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` has an `ignoreFailure: !requestStakeUpdate.toStake` which is correct, however when finalizing, the ignoreFailure is set to `true` instead of `!toStake`. This prevents the DSS from canceling the update if the vault changes somehow in the meantime.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

In `Operator::validateAndUpdateVaultStakeInDSS()` set `ignoreFailure` to `!queuedStakeUpdate.updateRequest.toStake`

```diff
    function validateAndUpdateVaultStakeInDSS(CoreLib.Storage storage self, QueuedStakeUpdate memory queuedStakeUpdate)
        external
    {
        State storage operatorState = self.operatorState[queuedStakeUpdate.operator];
        validateQueuedStakeUpdate(operatorState, queuedStakeUpdate);
        updateVaultStakeInDSS(
            operatorState,
            queuedStakeUpdate.updateRequest.vault,
            queuedStakeUpdate.updateRequest.dss,
            queuedStakeUpdate.updateRequest.toStake
        );
        delete operatorState.pendingStakeUpdates[queuedStakeUpdate.updateRequest.vault];
        IDSS dss = queuedStakeUpdate.updateRequest.dss;
        HookLib.callHookIfInterfaceImplemented({
            dss: dss,
            data: abi.encodeWithSelector(dss.finishUpdateStakeHook.selector, msg.sender),
            interfaceId: dss.finishUpdateStakeHook.selector,
-            ignoreFailure: true,
+            ignoreFailure: !queuedStakeUpdate.updateRequest.toStake
            hookCallGasLimit: self.hookCallGasLimit,
            supportsInterfaceGasLimit: self.supportsInterfaceGasLimit,
            hookGasBuffer: self.hookGasBuffer
        });
    }
```


## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/entities/Operator.sol#L126


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

`Core::finalizeUpdateVaultStakeInDSS()` can be called by anyone to finalize an update. It calls `validateAndUpdateVaultStakeInDSS()` to execute the state updates and in that function a callback is made to the DSS. In that callback we use low-level call to call the `finishUpdateStakeHook(address operator)` function, but instead of passing the operator the protocol passes `msg.sender` which can be anyone.

```solidity
    function validateAndUpdateVaultStakeInDSS(CoreLib.Storage storage self, QueuedStakeUpdate memory queuedStakeUpdate)
        external
    {
        ...
        HookLib.callHookIfInterfaceImplemented({
            dss: dss,
@->         data: abi.encodeWithSelector(dss.finishUpdateStakeHook.selector, msg.sender),
            interfaceId: dss.finishUpdateStakeHook.selector,
            ignoreFailure: true,
            hookCallGasLimit: self.hookCallGasLimit,
            supportsInterfaceGasLimit: self.supportsInterfaceGasLimit,
            hookGasBuffer: self.hookGasBuffer
        });
    }
```

The DSS will most likely take this argument and assume it is the operator which is not correct.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Change `msg.sender` to the operator of the vault.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/Vault.sol#L110-L119


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Vault shares can be easily inflated through donating assets. This means that when a user wants to mint shares, an attacker can front-run his transaction and donate tokens to the vault without minting any shares in exchange, this means the shares are now worth more since we have more assets, thus the user will have to pay more assets for the same amount of shares.

## Proof of Concept

Let's look at the following example:

- Bob wants to directly mint shares so he calls `Vault::mint(shares=100e18)`. The current exchange is 1e18 shares = 1e18 assets(1:1). Assume the vault is newly deployed and has low liquidity of let's say 500e18 tokens and 500e18 shares.
- A malicious user sees Bob's transaction and front-runs it by donating 500e18 assets in exchange for 0 shares. Now we have 1000e18 assets and 500e18 shares, meaning 1e18 shares = 2e18 assets(1:2).
- Assume Bob is planning to continuously deposit assets to the vault so he gives it a maximum approval, now his transaction executes and he pays 200e18 assets instead of 100e18.

This way the attecker successfully makes Bob pay more assets than he should have. This can easily be executed in low liquidity vaults.

Another thing to take into account here is that Bob doesn't want to use the deposit function with the slippage parameter because he allows some slippage. Let's say that he wanted to acquire 100e18 shares for a maximum of 150e18 assets(ideally 100e18 but he allows some slippage), then the `Vault::deposit(uint256 assets, address to, uint256 minSharesOut)` doesn't do the job and he has to use the mint function that currently has no slippage protection. This way Bob is tricked into supplying more than he wanted.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Adding a `maxAssets` to the `mint()` function will solve this issue.

```diff
-     function mint(uint256 shares, address to)
+     function mint(uint256 shares, address to, uint256 maxAssets)
        public
        override(ERC4626, IVault)
        whenFunctionNotPaused(Constants.PAUSE_VAULT_MINT)
        nonReentrant
        returns (uint256 assets)
    {
        if (shares == 0) revert ZeroShares();
        assets = super.mint(shares, to);
+       if(assets > maxAssets) revert ExceedsMaxAssets();
    }
```


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L430
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L299-L318


# Vulnerability details

The current slashing mechanism does not decrease user shares proportionally to the slashed assets, which is crucial because of the `convertToAssets()` calculations, and this leads to unintended penalties for users who are not affected by the slashing event. This can result in users being unfairly penalized, impacting their staking rewards.

## Impact

This vulnerability results in:

1. Unintended penalties for users not affected by the slashing event.
2. Reduced staking rewards for unaffected users.
3. Potential loss of confidence in the staking protocol due to unfair penalties.

## Proof of Concept

Let's suppose there are 3 stakers in the vault, and three users have staked ETH with the following details:

User 1: 32 ETH
User 2: 32 ETH
User 3: 32 ETH
Total Restaked ETH: 96 ETH
Total Assets: 96 ETH
Shares: 32, 32, 32
Total Shares: 96

User 1 gets slashed by 4 ETH.
The system updates the total assets but not the shares:

```solidity
    function slashAssets(uint256 totalAssetsToSlash, address slashingHandler)
        external
        onlyOwner
        nonReentrant
        whenFunctionNotPaused(Constants.PAUSE_NATIVEVAULT_SLASHER)
        returns (uint256 transferAmount)
    {
        NativeVaultLib.Storage storage self = _state();

        if (slashingHandler != self.slashStore) revert NotSlashStore();

        // avoid negative totalAssets if slashing amount is greater than totalAssets
        if (totalAssetsToSlash > self.totalAssets) {
            totalAssetsToSlash = self.totalAssets;
        }

        self.totalAssets -= totalAssetsToSlash;
        emit Slashed(totalAssetsToSlash);
        return totalAssetsToSlash;
    }
```

Total Restaked ETH: 32, 32, 32
Total Assets: 92 ETH
Shares: 32, 32, 32
Total Shares: 96

User 2, who has not been slashed, calculates their effective assets: function `_transferToSlashStore()`:

```solidity
        // slashed ETH = total restaked ETH (node + beacon) - share price equivalent ETH
        uint256 slashedAssets = node.totalRestakedETH - convertToAssets(balanceOf(nodeOwner));
```

This will be 32 - 32 * 92 / 96 = 32 - 30 = 2, so the `slashedAssets` is equal to 2, which then will be slashed from the contract:

```solidity
        // sweepable ETH = min(ETH available on node address, total slashed ETH)
        uint256 slashedWithdrawable = Math.min(node.nodeAddress.balance, slashedAssets);

        // withdraw sweepable ETH to slashStore
        INativeNode(node.nodeAddress).withdraw(self.slashStore, slashedWithdrawable);
```

Root Cause
The slashing function reduces the total assets but does not proportionally adjust the shares of the users. This imbalance causes unaffected users to experience a reduction in their effective assets during snapshots.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Modify the slashing function to reduce the shares of the affected user proportionally to the slashed amount.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Vault.sol#L94-L103


# Vulnerability details

The current `Vault.sol` contract includes slippage protection by specifying a minimum amount of shares to mint during deposits. However, it lacks a mechanism to set a deadline for these transactions, which can lead to exploits involving delayed transactions and slippage due to price changes.

When a transaction remains pending in the mempool for an extended period, it can be executed at an inopportune time, leading to significant slippage. This scenario is particularly dangerous for deposits and minting of shares, where the asset value may fluctuate.

```solidity
    function deposit(uint256 assets, address to, uint256 minSharesOut) // @audit not only slippage, they need deadline too
        external
        nonReentrant
        whenFunctionNotPaused(Constants.PAUSE_VAULT_DEPOSIT_SLIPPAGE)
        returns (uint256 shares)
    {
        if (assets == 0) revert ZeroAmount();
        shares = super.deposit(assets, to);
        if (shares < minSharesOut) revert NotEnoughShares();
    }
```

## Impact

The lack of a `deadline` for `deposit` and `mint` transactions allows them to remain pending in the mempool, becoming vulnerable to slippage and MEV attacks due to price fluctuations.

## Proof of Concept

1. Alice submits a transaction to deposit assets into the vault, specifying a minimum amount of shares to be minted to protect against slippage.
2. The transaction is submitted with a low gas fee and remains pending in the mempool.
3. While the transaction is pending, the price of the underlying asset changes significantly.
4. The minimum shares specified by Alice are now outdated due to the price change.
5. A MEV bot detects the pending transaction and takes advantage of the outdated slippage protection.
6. The bot manipulates the transaction to benefit from the price change, resulting in a significant loss for Alice.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Add slippage to the `mint` function and introduce a `deadline` parameter in the `deposit` and `mint` functions.


## Assessed type

Other

in [`CoreLib.cloneVault()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/CoreLib.sol#L149) the function makes a call like `LibClone.deployDeterministicERC1967BeaconProxy(address(this), salt)` which returns the deterministic address for the vault.

 however before this call is done executing there a few things that can go wrong i.e;
if you look in the `LibClone.deployDeterministicERC1967BeaconProxy` you'll see it calls an internal function `deployDeterministicERC1967BeaconProxy` with 3 parameters.
```solidity
    function deployDeterministicERC1967BeaconProxy(uint256 value, address beacon, bytes32 salt)
        internal
        returns (address instance)
    {
        /// @solidity memory-safe-assembly
        assembly {
            let m := mload(0x40) // Cache the free memory pointer.
            mstore(0x60, 0xb3582b35133d50545afa5036515af43d6000803e604d573d6000fd5b3d6000f3)
            mstore(0x40, 0x1b60e01b36527fa3f0ad74e5423aebfd80d3ef4346578335a9a72aeaee59ff6c)
            mstore(0x20, 0x60195155f3363d3d373d3d363d602036600436635c60da)
            mstore(0x09, or(shl(160, 0x60523d8160223d3973), shr(96, shl(96, beacon))))
            instance := create2(value, 0x0c, 0x74, salt)
@-->            if iszero(instance) {
                mstore(0x00, 0x30116425) // `DeploymentFailed()`.
                revert(0x1c, 0x04)
            }
            mstore(0x40, m) // Restore the free memory pointer.
            mstore(0x60, 0) // Restore the zero slot.
        }
    }
```
in that function we can see that after the create2 function execution the next line checks whether the value returned to `instance` is an address(0). 

However that is not a thorough check because whenever there is a failed deployment, it does not revert from the create2 opcode as it does not properly check the returned address for bytecode meaning the return value can be of a valid address but of `codesize = 0`, which is also invalid but our checks will not catch it 

## Tools Used
Manual review(Vs Code)

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
it is recommended to update iszero(result) to iszero(extcodesize(result)) or check size of code.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/entities/HookLib.sol#L55


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In the `HookLib.sol` the function `callHookIfInterfaceImplemented()` checks whether the `gasLeft()` is bigger than `(supportsInterfaceGasLimit * 64 / 63 + hookGasBuffer)`. However, the problem is that the check only multiplies gas limit for the function on 64/63 instead of multiplying the whole part along with the `hookGasBuffer`. The low-level call is performed with at most 63/64th of
the gas that the caller context has available. `hookGasBuffer` is as well gas available so not multiplying it by 64/63 means that the function doesn't make sure that the call is performed with at least gas available equal to gas limit plus gas buffer. 


## Proof of Concept

1. EIP-150 states that only 63/64th of the gas that the caller has forwarded for the call. 

2. In the current implementation of the hook functionality, only gas limit is multiplied by 64/63 not including the `gasBuffer` that is also included in the available gas for the call.

3. This leads to the check not being implemented correctly as it does not make sure that the function call is performed with 63/64th of the gas available. It only multiplies `supportsInterfaceGasLimit` and does not include `hookGasBuffer`.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Change the check on:

```
  if (gasleft() < (supportsInterfaceGasLimit + hookGasBuffer) * 64 / 63 ) {
            revert NotEnoughGas();
        }
```


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/Core.sol#L229


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In the current implementation of the `Core` smart contract, anybody can register DSS with implemented IDSS interface. It should only be a smart contract and it has to assign max slashing percentage. So a malicious operator can create its own DSS with slashing percentage == 100% and register to any other DSS with any slashing percentage. The problem is that when another DSS will request slashing, a malicious operator can front-run the tx by requesting the slashing from its own DSS and slash everything by himself.

## Proof of Concept

1. Operator registers his own DSS with slashing percentage == 100%.
2. Operator stakes his vault to another DSS with any percentage.
3. When another DSS requests slashing, operator front-runs the tx by slashing himself

In this scenario, the second DSS can be DoSed. Additionally, currently slashing handlers functionality is not unified and it's mostly custom so this problem can impact the future functionality if the slashed funds are transferred to another account or DSS itself instead of being burnt.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Check whether the leveraging works correctly and the vault is staked correctly with correct slashing percentages: for instance, vault cannot be staked in the DSS with slashing percentage == 70% if it's already staked in such DSS with the same slashing percentage.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/entities/SlasherLib.sol#L153


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In the current implementation of `Core` functionality, veto committee is supposed to put veto on the slashings that seem to be unfair. However, the problem is that the veto committee may be able to veto any time it wants after slashing request is created which can break the following invariant:

```
DSS can slash any malicious behavior occurring before the withdrawal initiation for up to 7 days.
```


## Proof of Concept

1. Let's say the DSS requested slashing and has waited for 2 days now it's able to slash during 7 days window according to the specification.

2. However, `cancelSlashing()` does not check whether the cancel operation is performed during `VETO_WINDOW` that allows to cancel anytime it wants:


https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/entities/SlasherLib.sol#L153-168
```
function cancelSlashing(CoreLib.Storage storage self, QueuedSlashing memory queuedSlashing) external {
        bytes32 slashRoot = calculateRoot(queuedSlashing);
        if (!self.slashingRequests[slashRoot]) revert InvalidSlashingParams();
        delete self.slashingRequests[slashRoot];
        IDSS dss = queuedSlashing.dss;

        HookLib.callHookIfInterfaceImplemented({
            dss: dss,
            data: abi.encodeWithSelector(dss.cancelSlashingHook.selector, queuedSlashing.operator),
            interfaceId: dss.cancelSlashingHook.selector,
            ignoreFailure: true,
            hookCallGasLimit: self.hookCallGasLimit,
            supportsInterfaceGasLimit: self.supportsInterfaceGasLimit,
            hookGasBuffer: self.hookGasBuffer
        });
    }
```

This effectively means that DSS may not have the whole 7 days to slash and the operation can be cancelled anytime during these 7 days.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Add the check to `cancelSlashing()` to make sure that `VETO_WINDOW` is still active and it's not interfere with actual slashing window.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

 https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/Core.sol#L118


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In the current implementation of the `Core` functionality, only operator can unregister himself from the DSS as `msg.sender` inside of `unregisterOperatorFromDSS` is operator. However, this goes in deviation with the specification regarding jailing implementation:

```
Jailing: Operators can be jailed by the DSS arbitrarily usually valid reasons like if they are too overleveraged for a DSS' liking
The effects of jailing are also arbitrary and can be decided by the DSS. This can range from no rewards to not allowing the operator to perform any tasks and forcing them to unallocate from the DSS. Jailing is optional and is implemented inside the DSS contract and not the core contract.
```

## Proof of Concept

Currently DSS cannot force an operator to unallocate from it as DSS is not the `msg.sender`:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/Core.sol#L113-118
```
 function unregisterOperatorFromDSS(IDSS dss, bytes memory unregistrationHookData)
        external
        nonReentrant
        whenFunctionNotPaused(Constants.PAUSE_CORE_UNREGISTER_FROM_DSS)
    {
        address operator = msg.sender;
```

So operator's vault can be staked inside of DSS whenever he wants even if the vault has no funds for slashing. This may put significant burden on DSS functionality as the operator will be in the system and still it'd not be possible to slash him. Therefore, such implementation where DSS cannot force operator to unallocate from it goes with deviation with the described intended behavior.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Add a function like `forceUnregisterOperatorFromDSS()` so that DSS can unregister operator itself in case of jailing.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

 https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/Core.sol#L259


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The current functionality in `Core` requires setting max slashable percentage from DSS to be considered registered. However, the DSS might want to set slashable percentage as 0% and do not slash any operators for anything. The problem is that in the current version of the code there is no any flag that indicates that DSS does not slash anything from the operators if it wants to which goes in deviation from the spec.

## Proof of Concept

Take a look at this comment:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/Core.sol#L258-261
```
/// @notice Allows the caller to register as a DSS and set the max slashable percentage
    /// @dev If you want to have 0% slashing, set `maxSlashablePercentageWad` to `1` since 0 is used as a default flag for not set
    /// If a operator is set, it will have a non-zero slashable percentage. Hence we can just check for that to see if a DSS is registered
```

Moreover, in the code review performed by the sponsors the same thing was said - that is DSS might want to not slash its operators and it has to specify 1 as `maxSlashablePercentageWad`. However, it's not the case, as when slashing event occurs, 1 in `maxSlashablePercentageWad` is treated exactly like 1%:


https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/entities/SlasherLib.sol#L85-90
```
  for (uint256 i = 0; i < slashingMetadata.vaults.length; ++i) {
            earmarkedStakes[i] = Math.mulDiv(
                slashingMetadata.slashPercentagesWad[i],
                IKarakBaseVault(slashingMetadata.vaults[i]).totalAssets(),
                Constants.MAX_SLASHING_PERCENT_WAD
            );
```

As you can see, the formula just multiplies slash percentage on total assets and divides by max slashing percentage. When validating slashing percentages, there is no any flag for 0% as well:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/entities/SlasherLib.sol#L54-55
```
 if (slashingRequest.slashPercentagesWad[i] == 0) revert ZeroSlashPercentageWad();
            if (slashingRequest.slashPercentagesWad[i] > maxSlashPercentageWad) revert MaxSlashPercentageWadBreached();

```

These are the only checks that are performed.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Set some additional flag for 0% slashing.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In the current implementation of the `Core` functionality, there is `MIN_STAKE_UPDATE_DELAY` parameter that is used to verify whether 9 days has passed since the vault stake update has been requested. ```
uint256 public constant MIN_STAKE_UPDATE_DELAY = SLASHING_WINDOW + SLASHING_VETO_WINDOW;

However, there can be a case when DSS does not validate an operator right away in `registerOperatorToDSS()` but does this in `validateAndUpdateVaultStakeInDSS()` after some time. The problem is that in the first function it does not ignore failure meaning DSS has an ability to block registration of operator but in the second function it cannot do so and it's just formal. Therefore, there is no any reason for such delay and it can significantly impact user experience and prevent from using it as it's needed to wait for 9 days to stake and 9 days to unstake a single vault.


## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Reduce update delay for staking operation as there are not any risks of front-running.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Core.sol#L264

# Vulnerability details

## Description 

In `Core.sol`, the function `registerDSS()` is designed to register a Decentralized Staking System (DSS) with the platform. Currently, this function checks if the caller is a smart contract by checking the code length at the caller's address. However, this method is not foolproof. With the widespread use of smart contracts and multisig wallets, it’s possible for malicious attacker to exploit this simple check, registering unauthorized DSS instances and potentially compromising the system’s integrity.

## Code

```solidity
function registerDSS(uint256 maxSlashablePercentageWad) external {
        IDSS dss = IDSS(msg.sender);
        if (!address(dss).isSmartContract()) revert NotSmartContract();
        _self().setDSSMaxSlashablePercentageWad(dss, maxSlashablePercentageWad);
        emit DSSRegistered(msg.sender, maxSlashablePercentageWad);
    }
```

## Impact

This vulnerability could allow unauthorized entities to register as DSS, potentially leading to security breaches or manipulation within the system. Malicious actors could exploit this loophole.

## Recommendation

To enhance security and ensure only legitimate DSS instances can register,the system should check for the implementation of a specific interface that bona fide DSS contracts would support. This approach adds an extra layer of validation, helping to confirm the identity and legitimacy of the caller.

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Core.sol#L220
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Core.sol#L235
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Vault.sol#L125
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Vault.sol#L157


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The current implementation allows a malicious operator to exploit the staking and redemption mechanisms. By staking a significant portion of their own vault (e.g., 50%) and then initiating the `startRedeem` process. Suppose after day 8 a DSS wants to slash about 80% of the vault but will not be able to do that because of the `SLASHING_VETO_WINDOW`. Till the veto period ends the operator can withdraw its stake and system will not be able to slash 80% but will be able to slash only 50% tokens.
This loophole allows the operator to withdraw funds before the slashing can be executed, effectively reducing the penalty. Add a mechanism where if the slashing request is in pending then don't allow to withdraw from that vault until slashing happens or Veto period finishes.

1. Malicious Operator Stake: The operator stakes a significant amount in their own vault, say 50%.
2. Initiate Redemption: The operator calls `startRedeem()` to begin the redemption process.
3. Malicious Activity Found: After 8 days, the operator found in malicious activity.
4. DSS Attempts Slashing: The DSS identifies the malicious behavior and initiates a slashing request for 70%.
5. Redemption Completion: However, due to the SLASHING_VETO_WINDOW, the DSS cannot execute the slashing immediately.
6. Withdrawal of Funds: The operator completes the redemption calling `finishRedeem` and withdraws their staked amount, leaving insufficient funds for the full slashing amount.

## Proof of Concept
![Screenshot 2024-07-31 010347](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ab2a8721-9970-4e94-900d-1555bfef73ca)
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/26b45229-7c2e-49bd-bc1d-efd11381d911)

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Block Withdrawals During Slashing Pending: Implement a mechanism that blocks withdrawals from the vault when a slashing request is pending. This would ensure that operators cannot withdraw funds once malicious activity is detected, allowing the DSS to execute the required slashing.


## Assessed type

Timing

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/ab18e1f6c03e118158369527baa2487b2b4616b1/src/NativeNode.sol#L39-L48


# Vulnerability details


## Proof of Concept

Take a look at https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/ab18e1f6c03e118158369527baa2487b2b4616b1/src/NativeNode.sol#L39-L48

```solidity
    function withdraw(address to, uint256 weiAmount)
        external
        onlyOwner
        nonReentrant
        whenFunctionNotPaused(Constants.PAUSE_NODE_WITHDRAW)
    {
        Address.sendValue(payable(to), weiAmount);
        emit NodeETHWithdrawn(address(this), to, weiAmount);
    }

```

This function allows the `NativeVault` to withdraw funds to the given address. As [documented](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/ab18e1f6c03e118158369527baa2487b2b4616b1/src/NativeNode.sol#L36), in the case of slashed assets the NativeVault withdraws those funds to the slashStore.

Issue however is that if we go to how slashings are being handled here https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/ab18e1f6c03e118158369527baa2487b2b4616b1/src/SlashingHandler.sol#L52-L59 we see that `safeTransfers()` inherently get called on these tokens.

This is also supported by the _### ERC20 token behaviors in scope_ here: https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/ab18e1f6c03e118158369527baa2487b2b4616b1/README.md#L146-L158, where we see that different sort of tokens could indeed be integrated.

Problem with the current logic is that the withdrawal hardcodes the logic to only allow withdrawal of ETH even though non-ETH tokens are supported, this is because the withdrawal context only uses `Address.sendValue()` as hinted by the `@audit` tag above, which then showcases a broken functionality cause some supported tokens won't be withdrawable.

## Impact

As hinted under _Proof of Concept_, some tokens have a broken functionality attached to them when trying to [withdraw the slashed assets](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/ab18e1f6c03e118158369527baa2487b2b4616b1/src/NativeNode.sol#L36), which is because the current functionality only allows for the withdrawal of native ETH via `sendValue()`

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider first checking if ETH is to be withdrawn in `NativeNode#withdraw()` then use `Address.sendValue(payable(to), weiAmount)` otherwise use `safeTransfer()` on the token.



## Assessed type

Context

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/entities/Operator.sol#L61-L76


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability

In `requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` when the ignoreFailure parameter is set to `!requestStakeUpdate.toStake`, it means that if the operator is staking (toStake is true), the hook cannot revert the transaction, and if the operator is unstaking (toStake is false), the hook can revert the transaction.

## Impact

DSS cannot enforce rule setting, malicious operators may be able to stake against rules. - Assets not a risk, but the function of the protocol or its availability could be impacted (See PoC Scenario #1)

Malicious DSS can hold operator funds hostage - Assets can be stolen/lost/compromised directly (See PoC Scenario #2)

## Proof of Concept
Scenario 1

1. A malicious operator, Eve, wants to stake in a DSS that has specific staking requirements and rules.
The DSS has implemented the `requestUpdateStakeHook` to enforce these rules and validate staking requests.
However, the `requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` function has the ignoreFailure parameter set to `!requestStakeUpdate.toStake`, allowing Eve to bypass the DSS's rule enforcement when staking.

2. Eve calls the `requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` function, passing the necessary parameters to initiate a staking request.
Since Eve is staking (`toStake` is true), the `ignoreFailure` parameter is set to true due to the bug.
The `requestUpdateStakeHook` is called on the DSS contract, but even if the DSS tries to revert the transaction due to Eve not meeting the staking requirements, the revert is ignored.
The staking request proceeds, and Eve successfully stakes in the DSS, bypassing the intended rule enforcement.

3. The DSS is unable to enforce its staking rules and requirements effectively.
Malicious operators like Eve can stake in the DSS even if they don't meet the specified criteria.

Scenario 2 

1. A malicious DSS wants to prevent operators from unstaking their funds, effectively holding their funds hostage.
The `requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` function has the `ignoreFailure` parameter set to `!requestStakeUpdate.toStake`, allowing the malicious DSS to revert unstaking requests.
An honest operator, Alice, has staked funds in the malicious DSS and now wants to unstake.

2. Alice calls the `requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` function, passing the necessary parameters to initiate an unstaking request.
Since Alice is unstaking (toStake is false), the `ignoreFailure` parameter is set to false due to the bug.
The `requestUpdateStakeHook` is called on the malicious DSS contract.
The malicious DSS takes advantage of this vulnerability and reverts the unstaking request in the hook, preventing Alice from unstaking her funds.
Alice's unstaking request fails, and her funds remain staked in the malicious DSS against her will.

3. The malicious DSS can hold operator funds hostage by reverting unstaking requests.
Operators like Alice are unable to unstake their funds when desired, losing control over their staked assets.
This vulnerability creates a significant risk for operators and undermines the trust and reliability of the staking ecosystem.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

it is crucial to correct the `ignoreFailure` parameter logic in the  `requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` function. The parameter should be set to `requestStakeUpdate.toStake` to ensure that the DSS can enforce its rules when staking and that operators can freely unstake their funds when desired.








## Assessed type

Error

# Lines of code

# Vulnerability details

In Vault.sol two of the functions are startRedeem() and finishRedeem(). Both functions are using convertToAssets() with parameter. This function is inherited from solmate. It is clear that convertToAssets() uses totalSupply. When totalSupply is used since it is very easy to manipulate there is a possibility for users of the protocol to lose funds. 

## Impact
Users may receive a worse price than expected for their shares when convertToAssets() is used. There's no protection at all for minimum return amount potentially leading to loss of user funds.

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Vault.sol#L137
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Vault.sol#L168

Bob may lose funds if the price per share change drastically during the whole redeem procedure.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Allow a user to specify a minOutAmount and make a check in startRedeem() and finishRedeem() in order to minimize the possibility of losing funds.

Token-Transfer

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/ab18e1f6c03e118158369527baa2487b2b4616b1/src/Vault.sol#L168
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/ab18e1f6c03e118158369527baa2487b2b4616b1/src/Vault.sol#L168


# Vulnerability details

## Description:

The current implementation of the Karak protocol relies on the `totalAssets()` function when converting assets to shares in the `convertToShares(...)` function and when converting shares to assets in the `convertToAssets(...)` function. This function returns the vault balance of the underlying asset, as shown below:

```solidity
function totalAssets() public view virtual returns (uint256 assets) {
    assets = SafeTransferLib.balanceOf(asset(), address(this));
}
```

However, a malicious attacker can manipulate the vault's token ratio and cause losses to stakers by transferring tokens directly to the vault address. This action increases the `totalAssets()` value without increasing the total supply of the vault token. As a result, whenever a staker redeems their shares, they will receive fewer assets than they should, with the excess remaining locked in the vault.

## Proof of Concept
```solidity
// SPDX-License-Identifier: SEE LICENSE IN LICENSE
pragma solidity ^0.8.25;

import "../../src/Vault.sol";
import "../helpers/OperatorHelper.sol";

contract AttackTests is OperatorHelper {
    Vault vault;

    function mintAndDepositBy(uint256 amount, address by) public returns (uint256 shares) {
        vm.startPrank(by);
        depositToken.mint(by, amount);
        depositToken.approve(address(vault), amount);
        uint256 expectedShares = vault.convertToShares(amount);
        shares = vault.deposit(amount, by, expectedShares);
        vm.stopPrank();
    }

    function setupDDs() public {
        stake_vaults_to_dss();
        vault = Vault(address(vaults[0]));
        vm.prank(operator);
        core.registerOperatorToDSS(dss2, "");
    }

    function deposit_and_withdraw(uint256 amountToDeposit, address by) public {
        uint256 shares = mintAndDepositBy(amountToDeposit, by);
        console.log("shares minted", shares);
        uint256 assetsToWithdrawPreeview = vault.previewRedeem(shares);
        uint256 shareToWithdrawPreeview = vault.previewWithdraw(amountToDeposit);
        console.log("Preview:Number of assets to be redeemed", assetsToWithdrawPreeview);
        console.log("Preview:Number of shares to be redeemed", shareToWithdrawPreeview);
        vm.startPrank(by);
        vault.approve(address(vault), shares);
        bytes32 withdrawalKey = vault.startRedeem(shares, by);

        vm.warp(block.timestamp + Constants.MIN_WITHDRAWAL_DELAY);
        vault.finishRedeem(withdrawalKey);
        uint256 balance = depositToken.balanceOf(address(vault));
        console.log("After redeeming the token");
        console.log("contract balance of the underlying", balance);
        uint256 totalSuply = vault.totalSupply();
        uint256 totalAssets = vault.totalAssets();

        console.log("totalSuply", totalSuply);
        console.log("totalAssets", totalAssets);
        vm.stopPrank();
    }

    function test_token_inflation() public {
        setupDDs();
        console.log("Before transfering the token to the vault");
        deposit_and_withdraw(100 wei, address(1));

        console.log("After transfering the token to the vault");

        depositToken.mint(address(this), 10 wei);
        depositToken.transfer(address(vault), 10 wei);
        for (uint256 i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
            deposit_and_withdraw(100 wei, address(1));
            deposit_and_withdraw(1000 wei, address(2));
            deposit_and_withdraw(100 wei, address(3));
            deposit_and_withdraw(1000 wei, address(4));
            deposit_and_withdraw(10000 wei, address(2));
            deposit_and_withdraw(1000 wei, address(3));
            deposit_and_withdraw(100000 wei, address(4));
        }
    }
}

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

If an allowed vault is found to be malicious in the future, it can be re-deploy for future `Vault` creation with his malicious behavior(s), which potentially impact all the users of Karak protocol. 

## Proof of Concept

The team/admin can allow a new implementation for the creation of `Vault` and `NativeVault`. Theses potentials new implementations are assumed to be audited and assumed safe by the team.

```solidity
    function allowlistVaultImpl(Storage storage self, address implementation) internal {
        self.allowlistedVaultImpl[implementation] = true;
    }
```
But if in the future we find an issue of a possible malicious bahevior in an added implementation. There are no way to remove an implementation in the `allowlistedVaultImpl` mapping.


For `Vault` and `NativeVault`, owner/admin can change the implementation address with `changeImplementationForVault()` but it can take time to make it and let a windows of time for malicious actions and it cost gas for the team. 
Undeniably, this can cause problems and a bad image for the protocol. 

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Add a way for the owner/admin to delete an implementation on the `allowlistedVaultImpl` mapping.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L334-L336
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L282


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

An operator can pause the `NativeNode::withdraw()` function which always revert when `finishWithdrawal()` is called and thus prevent the user from withdrawing his ETH.

## Proof of Concept

When an operator want to create a `NativeVault`, he call the `deployVaults()` function on the `Core` contract with a custom config struct to give informations for the deployment. The `extraData` params is used to give the `manager`, `slahsStore` and `nodeImplementation` addresses on the `initialize()` function of the `NativeVault`.

The operator set a `manager` role which can be useful for giving authority on some functions for a custom vault developed for specifics purposes.
We can see on the `NativeVault`, the owner and also the manager can [pause](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L334-L336) the `NativeNode` functions:

```solidity
    function pauseNode(INativeNode node, uint256 map) external onlyRolesOrOwner(Constants.MANAGER_ROLE) {
        node.pause(map);
    }
```

If the manager pause the `withdraw()` function on the `NativeNode`, it create a DoS of the withdrawal process, because when the user try to finalize a withdrawal, the call will always [revert](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L282).

We can also note than also when the `withdraw()` function is paused, it's impossible to make a snapshot of the `NativeVault`.

At the end, the protocol can unpause the `withdraw()` function and revoke the manager privilege on the `NativeVault` to let the user withdraw, this issue is considered as a temporary freezing of funds.
Note that if the administrator/team needs to revoke the manager privilege, the functionality of the custom manager authority on a custom vault is broken.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
In my opinion you can delete the `whenFunctionNotPaused` modifier on the `NativeNode::withdraw()` function to avoid potentials malicious behavior of the manager role.


## Assessed type

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/entities/HookLib.sol#L55
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/entities/HookLib.sol#L87


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The transaction may revert when trying to call a DSS hook while it should not.

## Proof of Concept

The function `HookLib::callHook()` and `HookLib::callHookIfInterfaceImplemented()` start by making sure the `gasleft()` is enough to execute the corresponding hook on a DSS by following the 63/64 rule.

This rule stipulates an external call forwards 63/64 of the gas left and keeps 1/64 of the gas left to proceed the last part of the transaction once the external call succeeded.

In the mentioned functions, in case the gas that will be forwarded is not enough, the transaction reverts early.

Here is how `callHook()` estimates the gas the hook costs.

```solidity
if (gasleft() < (hookCallGasLimit * 64 / 63 + hookGasBuffer)) revert NotEnoughGas();
```

This formula does not calculate the gas accurately.

The calculation returns a value greater than it should meaning the transactions will most likely revert while they should not.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Reverse the `63` and `64` values in the corresponding formulas

*callHook()*

```diff
- if (gasleft() < (hookCallGasLimit * 64 / 63 + hookGasBuffer)) revert NotEnoughGas();
+ if (gasleft() < (hookCallGasLimit * 63 / 64 + hookGasBuffer)) revert NotEnoughGas();
```

*callHookIfInterfaceImplemented()*

```diff
- if (gasleft() < (supportsInterfaceGasLimit * 64 / 63 + hookGasBuffer)) {
-     revert NotEnoughGas();
- }

+ if (gasleft() < (supportsInterfaceGasLimit * 63 / 64 + hookGasBuffer)) {
+     revert NotEnoughGas();
+ }
```


## Assessed type

Error

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Let's look at this using the Core.sol.registerDSS() function as an example:

The Core.sol.registerDSS() function allows the caller to register as a DSS and set the max slashable percentage. The function receives the maxSlashablePercentageWad parameter,
which means "The max slashable percent, in the form of wad, that the DSS can slash per cooldown period". This parameter is set for
DSS msg.sender:

IDSS dss = IDSS(msg.sender);
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/Core.sol#L263

However, this can be bypassed. You can set the DSS for any address to any maxSlashablePercentageWad value. You can also change the maxSlashablePercentageWad
for an existing DSS.

## Proof of Concept
You can call the SlasherLib.setDSSMaxSlashablePercentageWad() function directly with your parameters:
CoreLib.Storage storage self,
IDSS dss,
uint256 dssMaxSlashablePercentageWad
The SlasherLib.setDSSMaxSlashablePercentageWad() function does not check that the calling address msg.sender owns this DSS.

The same applies to the functions:
Core.requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS() and Operator.requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS();
Core.registerOperatorToDSS() and Operator.registerOperatorToDSS();
Core.unregisterOperatorFromDSS() and Operator.unregisterOperatorFromDSS();
Core.cancelSlashing() and SlasherLib.cancelSlashing().

## Tools Used
Manual review

Add a check to the SlasherLib.setDSSMaxSlashablePercentageWad() function that the calling address msg.sender owns this DSS. Similarly, for the functions:
Core.requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS() and Operator.requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS();
Core.registerOperatorToDSS() and Operator.registerOperatorToDSS();
Core.unregisterOperatorFromDSS() and Operator.unregisterOperatorFromDSS();

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Vault.sol#L78


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The deposit function in the Vault contract calls the `deposit` function of the ERC4626 contract, which transfers assets from the Vault contract. This process assumes that the Vault contract already holds the assets intended for deposit, which creates a vulnerability. A malicious user can observe the legitimate user's transaction in the mempool(transferring asset to vault contract) and execute a transaction just after the legitimate user’s transaction which transferred asset in vault and executing attacker/miner transaction before user calls `deposit`, causing the legitimate user to lose funds and revert. The issue arises because both the transfer and deposit operations cannot be done atomically by an externally owned account (EOA).
results in Loss of Funds: Legitimate users can lose their assets if their deposit transactions are front-run and manipulated by malicious users.

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Vault.sol#L78

Step 1: Legitimate User’s Actions:
User A prepares a transaction to transfer 100 tokens to the Vault contract.
User A prepares a transaction to call the deposit function with 100 tokens.

Step 2: Malicious User’s Actions:
User B monitors the mempool and identifies User A’s pending transfer and deposit transactions.
User B quickly prepares a transaction to call the deposit function with 100 tokens with high gas fee, front-running User A's deposit transaction.

Step 3: Attack Execution:
User B’s transaction is executed first, transferring shares from the Vault contract to User B.
User A's deposit transaction is executed, but the shares have already been minted to User B.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To prevent this issue, implement a solution that ensures atomic transfer and deposit operations.

Modify the deposit function to handle the asset transfer internally, ensuring that the assets are transferred from the user's address directly to the vault during the deposit call.



## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Vault.sol#L125
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Vault.sol#L168


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The startRedeem and finishRedeem functions in the vault contract enable users to redeem their assets. However, there is a significant issue due to the way assets are calculated at different times during the process. The startRedeem function uses the convertToAssets function to determine the amount of assets equivalent to the shares being redeemed, based on the totalAssets at the time of the call. This amount is recorded and emitted in an event.

However, the `finishRedeem` function, which can be called after a delay (e.g., 9 days), also calls `convertToAssets` to determine the redeemable assets based on the current totalAssets. Since the totalAssets can change over time due to deposits, withdrawals, and other activities, the amount of assets calculated during `finishRedeem` can differ significantly from what was calculated during `startRedeem`.

As the time constraint is used to stop the staker to not front-run the slashing process but totalSupply can also effect the asset calculations.
also the amount of asset event emitted in `startredeem` can be different from the the actual asset minted in `finishredeem`

Inaccurate Redemption: Users may receive a different amount of assets than what was calculated and recorded during startRedeem, leading to potential losses

## Proof of Concept

Step 1: User Starts Redeem:
A user initiates the redeem process by calling `startRedeem` with a certain number of shares.
The `convertToAssets` function calculates the amount of assets based on the totalAssets at that time.
```javascript
uint256 assets = convertToAssets(shares);

```

Step 2: totalAssets Changes:
Over the next few days, other users deposit and withdraw assets, changing the totalAssets of the vault.

Step 3: User Finishes Redeem:
After the required delay, the user calls finishRedeem to complete the redemption.
The convertToAssets function calculates the redeemable assets based on the current totalAssets.
```javascript
uint256 redeemableAssets = convertToAssets(shares);

```
Result:

If totalAssets has increased due to new deposits, the user will receive more assets than initially calculated.
If totalAssets has decreased (e.g., due to withdrawals), the user will receive fewer assets, potentially leading to a revert if the assets are insufficient.

## Tools Used
manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
carefully design the asset calculations function again.


## Assessed type

## Impact
The `requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` function allows an operator to either stake or unstake a vault to/from a DSS (Decentralized Staking System). The StakeUpdateRequest struct includes a boolean field, toStake, which indicates whether the operator intends to stake (true) or unstake (false) the vault.

Within the `requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` function, the callHookIfInterfaceImplemented is invoked to handle hooks if implemented by the DSS. One of the parameters for this function, ignoreFailure, is set to the negation of `requestStakeUpdate.toStake`

```javascript
 ignoreFailure: !requestStakeUpdate.toStake
```

This means that if the operation is a stake (toStake is true), ignoreFailure is set to false, and if the operation is an unstake (toStake is false), ignoreFailure is set to true.
Inconsistent Behavior: Depending on the implementation of the hook in the DSS, this could lead to inconsistent behavior where the hook call may fail silently during unstaking but not during staking. This might not be the intended functionality and can cause logical errors or unintended side effects.

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/Operator.sol#L82
Stake Request:
When requestStakeUpdate.toStake is true, ignoreFailure is set to false.
The hook call will not ignore failures, meaning any failure during the staking hook execution will propagate.
```javascript 
ignoreFailure: !requestStakeUpdate.toStake  // translates to ignoreFailure: false
```
Unstake Request:

When requestStakeUpdate.toStake is false, ignoreFailure is set to true.
The hook call will ignore failures, meaning any failure during the unstaking hook execution will be ignored.
```javascript
ignoreFailure: !requestStakeUpdate.toStake  // translates to ignoreFailure: true

 ```

## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Ensure the ignoreFailure parameter aligns with the intended functionality of the protocol. If failures should not be ignored during either operation, remove the negation. or vice versa
```javascript 
ignoreFailure: false

```

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/HookLib.sol#L28


# Vulnerability details

## Summary

The HookLib.sol is responsible for calling hooks on the DSS contract. Before calling one, it uses the ERC165 to validate that the DSS contract supports the function selector that will be called as a hook. However, the implementation does not follow Ethereum's [ERC165 standard.](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-165)

## Vulnerability Details

In the details of the Karak audit page on CodeArena, it states that:
```
EIP compliance checklist
- DSS contract should comply with ERC-165.
```

The ERC165 standard states that the call to the supportsInterface method should be a `STATICCALL` for security, ensuring that the call won't modify the state. However, in the current implementation in HookLib.sol, the performLowLevelCallAndLimitReturnData uses `CALL` instead of `STATICCALL`.

```solidity
    function performLowLevelCallAndLimitReturnData(address target, bytes memory data, uint256 gasLimit)
        internal
        returns (bool success, bytes32 returnVal)
    {
        bytes32[1] memory returnData;

        assembly {
            // pointer(data) + 0x20 is where actual data is available
            // pointer(data) contains the size of the data in bytes
            // returnData is where the return value is written to
            // we limit size of return value to 32 bytes (same as the size of `returnData` above)
            success :=
 @>>            call(
                    gasLimit, // gas available to the inner call
                    target, // address of contract being called
                    0, // ETH (denominated in WEI) being transferred in this call
                    add(data, 0x20), // Pointer to actual data (i.e. 32 bytes offset from `data`)
                    mload(data), // Size of actual data (i.e. the value stored in the first 32 bytes at `data`)
                    returnData, // Free pointer as a buffer for the inner call to write the return value
                    32 // 32 bytes size limit for the return value
                )
        }
        returnVal = returnData[0];
    }
```

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommendations

Comply to ERC-165 by using `STATICCALL` instead of `CALL`



## Assessed type

Context

# Lines of code

# Vulnerability details

## Summary

The decision on how to distribute rewards lies with the DSS, and in the DeFi sector, it's typical for the amount restaked to be proportional to the Operator's rewards. It’s reasonable to expect DSSes to favor this approach. However, if the NativeVault's totalAssets do not accurately reflect the restaked Ethereum, rewards distribution could end up being unfair.

## Vulnerability Details
If an Operator’s validator (represented by NativeNodes) is slashed at the snapshot's start by the beacon chain and the balance snapshotProof for the validator has been already submitted, the NativeVault’s totalAssets remain unchanged. This is because new proof submissions must wait 7 days due to the constraints of not validating validators twice in one active snapshot. This is enforced by the code snippet below, in [validateSnapshotProofs()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L150)

```solidity
   if (validatorDetails.lastBalanceUpdateTimestamp >= node.currentSnapshotTimestamp) {
       revert ValidatorAlreadyProved();
    }
```

Here's a revised version without using "warranted":

---

This issue also applies when one or more validators fully withdraw. Both full withdrawals and significant slashing events from the beacon chain can drastically affect the assets, potentially impacting them by 100s of ETH when multiple validators are involved. Consequently, any rewards distributed by the DSS during this period could be higher than appropriate, or just any system that relies on the accuracy of the restaked amount, could have complications.

Ideally, the safest time to distribute rewards would be after the snapshot proof has been submitted. However, since a slash targets the NativeVault itself and could potentially involve hundreds of validators, there is no perfectly safe time to distribute rewards. The accuracy of totalAssets is likely to decrease as more validators are added.

It should not fall upon the DSS to find the perfect timing for distributing rewards, instead, it is the responsibility of the NativeVault to ensure the accuracy of data. This cannot be achieved by limiting balance update proofs to the current frequency.

EigenLayer's Restaking protocol addresses those problems by allowing the [EigenPod](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol) which is similar to NativeNode, to receive constant updates. 

> _Other potential issues include the overall security of the protocol being compromised by infrequent updates of actual restaked assets. Not having up-to-date information about the amount of ETH an Operator contributes can limit the DSS's ability to act promptly if assets significantly decrease after proofs submissions._

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommendations

To mitigate such issues effectively, it would be beneficial to enable more frequent updates of a validator's balance, rather than limiting updates to once per snapshot every 7 days. A commendable example is the approach taken by EigenPod, which facilitates more dynamic balance management. - [EigenPod](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol)

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/NativeVaultLib.sol#L121-L122

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
the ```validateSnapshotProof``` function calculates ```balanceDeltaWei``` as the difference between ```newBalanceWei``` and ```prevBalanceWei```, both of which are uint256. The calculation is performed using int256 to handle the possibility of a negative difference.
## Proof of Concept
Consider the following scenario:
```prevBalanceWei``` is a uint256 with a value of (2^{255}) (which is within the valid range for uint256).
```newBalanceWei``` is also a uint256 and has a value slightly higher, say (2^{255} + 100).

When these values are converted to int256:
```int256(prevBalanceWei)``` will convert (2^{255}) correctly since it's the boundary value.
```int256(newBalanceWei)``` will overflow because (2^{255} + 100) exceeds the maximum positive value for an int256.
The overflow turns the value into a negative number in the int256 representation, which is not the intended behavior and can lead to incorrect calculations of balanceDeltaWei.
## Tools Used
manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
you should ensure that values being converted from uint256 to int256` do not exceed (2^{255} - 1). by for putting checks like
```solidity
require(prevBalanceWei <= uint256(type(int256).max), "prevBalanceWei too large");
require(newBalanceWei <= uint256(type(int256).max), "newBalanceWei too large");
