# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L451


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Any User can stop the "slashed assets" from being transferred from their nativenode to the `slashstore`. This would cause a loss of funds for the contract.

## Proof of Concept
In Native Restaking, any user (having >0 active validators) can start a snapshot which will update the `node.currentSnapshotTimestamp` of the user. Following this the users assets cannot be transferred out of the `native.node`. Even if the `validateExpiredSnapshot()` function is called by someone, it calls the `_startSnapshot()` function which has the following checks:

`if (node.currentSnapshotTimestamp != 0) revert PendingIncompleteSnapshot();`

Since the user has started a snapshot and not ended it (which he is not compelled to do), this check will cause the `_startSnapshot()` function to always revert. 

Since the slashedAsset transfer and calculation for a user is done inside the `_startSnapshot()` function, this makes it impossible for the nativeVault contract to transfer funds of the nativenode to the slashstore. And since the `withdraw()` function in the nativenode contract can be called only by the nativevault, the funds can never be transferred to the slashstore, thus causing a loss of funds for the contract.

## Tools Used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
One way to mitigate this is to keep a time limit on how long a snapshot can remain open.
for example adding this check in the `_startSnapshot()` function:

`if (node.currentSnapshotTimestamp !=0 && node.currentSnapshotTimestamp + MAX_SNAPSHOT_TIME_PERIOD < block.timestamp)` // Added check
`{`
    `delete node.currentSnapshotTimestamp;`
    `delete node.currentSnapshot;`
`}`
`if (node.currentSnapshotTimestamp != 0) revert PendingIncompleteSnapshot();` // existing check




## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L425-L446
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L482-L484

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/NativeVaultLib.sol#L127-L129


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
A slashing scenario in which users would lose more(double) than the intended slashed amount.

## Proof of Concept
Assume the following scenario (for mathematical simplicity assuming that BOB is the first and the only user of the vault):
1. ***Bob creates a node, and adds 2 validators each with 32ETH as balance***
(Bob.totalRestakedEth = 64ETH, self.totalAssets = 64ETH)
2. ***The NativeVault is slashed for 30ETH***
(self.totalAssets = 64 - 34 = 34ETH)
3. ***Bob withdraws from the validators and thus the funds are transferred to the native node***
(bobs_node.balance = 64ETH)
4. ***Bob calls the `startSnapshot()` function, here the following things are calculated:***
***In the _transferToSlashStore() function:***(https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L425-L446)
(30ETH is transferred from Bob's native node to slashstore,
Bobs totalRestakedETH = 34ETH)

5. ***Bob calls the `validateSnapshotProofs()` function, here the following things are calculated:***
***In the `_updateSnapshot()` function:*** (https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L482-L484)
(totalDeltaWei = 34 + (-64) = -30ETH)

***In the `_decreaseBalance()` function called thereafter:***(https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L512-L513)
(self.totalAssets = 34 - 30 = 4ETH,
self.ownerToNode[_of].totalRestakedETH = 34 - 30 = 4ETH)

This is wrong since, only 30ETH should have been reduced from the initial 64ETH, but here we can see that 30*2 = 60ETH is being reduced from the user.

## Tools Used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
A different approach may have to be implemented for the fully withdrawal condition.(Many changes would have to be brought here: https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/NativeVaultLib.sol#L127-L129)

Math

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L439


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In Native Restaking, users `totalRestakedETH` can be reduced prematurely thus reducing his potential rewards.

## Proof of Concept
After a slashing is done on the native vault, the slashed amount is collected from the users according to how much ETH is present in their native nodes, and the rest is collected in the following snapshots when their balance increases. 

But an attacker can transfer the entire supposed "slashed_amount" of the user to him via the requestOwnershipHandover() function in Ownable.sol that the NativeNode contract is inheriting. This would cause the `totalRestakedETH` amount to be reduced by the entire "slashed_amount".

# Path
Assume the following scenario
1. Bob has `totalRestakedETH = 32 ETH`, amounting to 50% of the totalAssets, and 0ETH as node.balance (in his nativenode)

2. The NativeVault is slashed for 20ETH, which means Bob must be slashed 10ETH

# Scenario 1 (No attack)
3. Bob calls the `startSnapshot()` function, and the function doesnt transfer anything to the slashstore since his node.balance = 0. Which means Bobs reward until next snapshot will be calculate with `totalRestakedETH = 32 ETH` since `slashedWithdrawable = 0`.

# Scenario 2 (attack)
3. A malicious attacker transfers 10ETH to bobs native node by calling the `requestOwnershipHandover()` payable function in the Ownable contract which native node is inheriting.

After a user creates a native node, and proceeds to call the `validateWithdrawalCredentials()` function, any user can frontrun this transaction and call the `validateExpiredSnapshot()` function. `{`
            `revert SnapshotNotExpired();`

`if (`

Manual

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L228-L294


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
User can completely escape being slashed in most cases.

## Proof of Concept
A user can continue creating multiple withdrawals (by calling the `startWithdrawal()` function) as his `withdrawableWei()` keeps increasing, and when a slashing occurs, he can frontrun this and withdraw his staked amount.

## Example (when 
1. Bob has 10ETH as withdrawableWei().
2. Bob creates a withdrawal with weiAmount = 10ETH
3. After 9 days (`MIN_WITHDRAWAL_DELAY`) this would mature, and Bob will be able to frontrun any future slashing event and completely withdraw his eth.
4. After a snapshot his withdrawableWei() increases by 5ETH
5. Bob can create another withdrawal with weiAmount = 5ETH, and be immune to slashing after 9 days.

The only scenario in which Bob is unable to escape slashing is when he is slashed within 9 days of starting a withdrawal which should be a rare occurrence since slashing is something that ideally happens rarely.

Do note that even though in this scenario, the amount in the validator can be slashed during withdrawal, this won't work if Bob's restaked eth is all present in the native node (by doing a fully withdrawal from the validator to the native node prior to the example given above) thus making it possible for anyone to do this attack.
## Tools Used
Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
One way to mitigate this is to keep a time limit on how long a withdrawal can be kept open.
This can be done by adding the following check at line 277 in nativevault.sol:
`if (startedWithdrawal.start + Constants.MAX_WITHDRAWAL_TIME < block.timestamp)`
`revert MaxWithdrawableTimePassed();`

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/NativeVault.sol#L25


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
None of the vaults protocol contracts include a __gap variable. Without this variable, it is not possible to add any new variables to the inherited contracts without causing storage slot issues. Specifically, if variables are added to an inherited contract, the storage slots of all subsequent variables in the contract will shift by the number of variables added. Such a shift would likely break the contract

## Proof of Concept
[src/Vault.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/Vault.sol#L29)
[src/NativeVault.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/NativeVault.sol#L25)
```solidity
import {Initializable} from "@openzeppelin-upgradeable/proxy/utils/Initializable.sol";  <@

import {Pauser} from "./entities/Pauser.sol";
import {VaultLib} from "./entities/VaultLib.sol";
import {WithdrawLib} from "./entities/Withdraw.sol";

function initialize( <@
    address _owner,
    address _operator,
    address _depositToken,
    string memory _name,
    string memory _symbol,
    bytes memory _extraData
) external initializer {
    _initializeOwner(_owner);
    __Pauser_init();
```

According to above code we can see vaults is upgradeable protocol.

The Vault and NativeVault contract are intended to be used as logic contracts with a proxy, but do not have a __gap variable. This would become problematic if a subsequent version was to inherit one of these contracts. If the derived version were to have storage variables itself and additional storage variables were subsequently added to the inherited contract, a storage collision would occur.


## Tools Used
Foundry
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider appending a __gap variable as the last storage variable to these upgradeable contracts

Upgradable

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/Vault.sol#L125
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/Vault.sol#L157
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/entities/SlasherLib.sol#L129


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
An operator can create a Race Condition between his withdrawal request and the DSS's slash request, allowing him to avoid slashing after a slashable offense. This is possible due to the slash delay, `SLASHING_VETO_WINDOW`, imposed on the DSS. The comment in the vault contract states, `"To prevent someone from sitting on queuedWithdrawals to front-run a slashing, DSS shouldn't consider stakes queued in withdrawals."` Unfortunately, an operator can, after joining a DSS, create a withdrawal request via `startRedeem()`. By doing this, the DSS has more than likely counted all of the operator's stake since the `queuedWithdrawals` is created after joining the DSS. 

The operator's withdrawal request takes 9 days to process while the DSS slash request takes 2 days. 

```solidity
 uint256 public constant SLASHING_WINDOW = 7days;

...snip...

uint256 public constant SLASHING_VETO_WINDOW = 2 days;

...snip...

uint256 public constant MIN_WITHDRAWAL_DELAY = SLASHING_WINDOW + SLASHING_VETO_WINDOW;

```

On its face, this should be fine but if an operator commits the slashable offense with less than 2 days left for his withdrawal request to finish processing the DSS will be unable to slash him in time since the DSS has to wait at least two days before slashing.

```solidity
function finalizeSlashing(CoreLib.Storage storage self, QueuedSlashing memory queuedSlashing) external {

        bytes32 slashRoot = calculateRoot(queuedSlashing);

        if (!self.slashingRequests[slashRoot]) revert InvalidSlashingParams();

        if (queuedSlashing.timestamp + Constants.SLASHING_VETO_WINDOW > block.timestamp) {

            revert MinSlashingDelayNotPassed();

        }

...snip...

```

As a result, an operator can create a Race Condition between his withdrawal request and the DSS's slash request, allowing him to avoid slashing after a slashable offense.

## Proof of Concept

Operator after registering with DSS creates a withdrawal request via `startRedeem()`.

Operator waits for 9 days.

Operator performs a slashable offense. 

DSS detects slashable offense committed by the operator and calls. `requestSlashing()`.

Operator calls `finishRedeem()` to withdraw his assets

DSS was unable to successfully slash the Operator before his withdrawal request was executed because the DSS had to wait `SLASHING_VETO_WINDOW ` or 2 days. 

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
When a DSS submits a Slash Request the operator's Withdrawal Request should be cancelled or rescheduled. 


## Assessed type

Timing

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Time sensitive slashing for the Operator wouldn't be possible for the DSS, as the finalize slashing method has to wait for 2 days before the next request slashing is approved 

## Proof of Concept
The request slashing method in slasher lib, allows to request the slashing of an operator, but the return value and success boolean of the request to DSS is ignored.

In the case where the transaction is reverted. Slashing requests cannot be made and the finalize slashing method will fail silently and the request would have to be made again in 2 days. 

```solidity
        HookLib.callHookIfInterfaceImplemented({
            dss: dss,
            data: abi.encodeWithSelector(
                dss.requestSlashingHook.selector, slashingMetadata.operator, slashingMetadata.slashPercentagesWad

            //@audit
@>            ignoreFailure: true,
            hookCallGasLimit: self.hookCallGasLimit,
            supportsInterfaceGasLimit: self.supportsInterfaceGasLimit,
            hookGasBuffer: self.hookGasBuffer
        });
```
This delay would give the operator more time to grief the protocol.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/NativeVault.sol#L168-L204


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
It is impossible to update the validator's balance in future snapshots as the number of active validators for all native nodes will always remain at 0.

## Proof of Concept

Node owners invoke the [`NativeVault::validateWithdrawalCredentials()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/NativeVault.sol#L168C2-L204C6) function to add active validators to their native node:

```solidity
for (uint256 i = 0; i < validatorFieldsProofs.length; i++) {
            totalRestakedWei += self.validateWithdrawalCredentials(
                nodeOwner,
                beaconStateRootProof.timestamp,
                beaconStateRootProof.beaconStateRoot,
                validatorFieldsProofs[i]
            );
        }
```

However, after calling [`NativeVault::validateWithdrawalCredentials()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/NativeVault.sol#L168C2-L204C6) to add all active validators in the loop above, the function does not increase the node.activeValidatorCount (i.e., the number of active validators in a native node) by the number of newly added validators.
This makes it impossible to update the validator's balance in future snapshots as the number of active validators for all native nodes will always remain at 0.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Increment node.activeValidatorCount by the number of active validators:

```diff
       for (uint256 i = 0; i < validatorFieldsProofs.length; i++) {
            totalRestakedWei += self.validateWithdrawalCredentials(
                nodeOwner,
                beaconStateRootProof.timestamp,
                beaconStateRootProof.beaconStateRoot,
                validatorFieldsProofs[i]
            );
        }
+        node.activeValidatorCount += validatorFieldsProofs.length;
        _increaseBalance(nodeOwner, totalRestakedWei);
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/NativeVault.sol#L285


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Due to the incorrect resetting of `withdrawalMap[withdrawalKey]`, a malicious user can repeatedly call [`NativeVault::finishWithdrawal()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/NativeVault.sol#L262) with the same `withdrawalKey` to withdraw all their assets, effectively bypassing the `MIN_WITHDRAWAL_DELAY`.



## Proof of Concept

In the M-1 of the [Renascence report](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/audits/eth-native-restaking/Renascence%20-%20Karak%20Native%20Restaking%20Audit%20Report.pdf) the following fix was implemented to reset the `withdrawalMap[withdrawalKey]` storage:

```diff
_decreaseBalance(startedWithdrawal.nodeOwner, startedWithdrawal.assets);
        INativeNode(node.nodeAddress).withdraw(startedWithdrawal.to, startedWithdrawal.assets);
        node.withdrawableCreditedNodeETH -= startedWithdrawal.assets;

+        delete self.withdrawalMap[withdrawalKey];
```

The issue is that `withdrawalMap` is a nested mapping in the [`Storage struct`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/entities/NativeVaultLib.sol#L90) and will not be reset this way. The `delete` operation does not traverse nested mappings as it lacks key set information.

Thus, the fix in the [Renascence report](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/audits/eth-native-restaking/Renascence%20-%20Karak%20Native%20Restaking%20Audit%20Report.pdf) has introduced a new issue that needs to be mitigated.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

As I am not sure of the best way to mitigate the vulnerability, I prefer to let the protocol decide the potential fix.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L443-L445


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
When there is a slash operation in NativeVault, call `NativeVault::startSnapshot()` with `revertIfNoBalanceChange` set to `true` will always revert even balance is changed.
Here before make a snapshot, the code will first check [whether the vault is slashed](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L456), if it is [slashed](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L430), then the slashed ETH will be withdraw to `slashStore` which means `node.nodeAddress.balance` will decrease.Because `node.withdrawableCreditedNodeETH` is actually the sum of `snapshot.nodeBalanceWei` and `snapshot.nodeBalanceWei` is actually the [diff between `node.nodeAddress.balance` and `node.withdrawableCreditedNodeETH`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L459) So 
`node.withdrawableCreditedNodeETH` is logically equal to `node.nodeAddress.balance`.When `node.nodeAddress.balance` decreases, the code will go to line 444, which will make them equal again.
Here the balance clearly changed, but in line 459 and 461 the `nodeBalanceWei` will be zero because in the above step we make `node.nodeAddress.balance` equal to `node.withdrawableCreditedNodeETH` already.So the function will revert even if the balance has clearly changed.

## Proof of Concept

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L272-L274
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L228-L294


# Vulnerability details

The `NativeVault` contract allows users to start a withdrawal request using the `startWithdrawal` function, specifying the recipient address and the amount of ETH to withdraw. This function records the withdrawal request details, including the start timestamp, in the `withdrawalMap` mapping.

To complete a withdrawal, the `finishWithdrawal` function is called with the corresponding `withdrawalKey`. This function is supposed to enforce a minimum withdrawal delay, ensuring that a certain amount of time has passed since the withdrawal request was started before allowing it to be finished.

However, the current implementation of `finishWithdrawal` does not properly enforce the minimum withdrawal delay. The issue lies in the following lines: [#L272-L274](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L272-L274)

```solidity
if (startedWithdrawal.start + Constants.MIN_WITHDRAWAL_DELAY > block.timestamp) {
    revert MinWithdrawDelayNotPassed();
}
```

The condition `startedWithdrawal.start + Constants.MIN_WITHDRAWAL_DELAY > block.timestamp` is incorrect. It allows the withdrawal to be finished if the current timestamp exceeds the start timestamp plus the minimum withdrawal delay. However, this condition should be reversed to ensure that the minimum withdrawal delay has passed before the withdrawal is finished.

_As a result, an attacker can bypass the withdrawal delay enforcement by calling `finishWithdrawal` immediately after starting a withdrawal request, effectively allowing them to withdraw funds without waiting for the intended delay period._

## Impact

The incorrect withdrawal delay enforcement in `finishWithdrawal` allows users to bypass the minimum withdrawal delay and withdraw funds immediately after starting a withdrawal request. This violates the intended behavior of the contract and can lead to premature withdrawal of funds, potentially impacting the contract's liquidity and the expected time-lock on withdrawals.

## Proof of Concept

1. User starts a withdrawal request by calling `startWithdrawal`, specifying the recipient address and the amount of ETH to withdraw.
2. The `startWithdrawal` function records the withdrawal request details, including the start timestamp, in the `withdrawalMap` mapping.
3. Immediately after starting the withdrawal request, the user calls `finishWithdrawal` with the corresponding `withdrawalKey`.
4. Due to the incorrect condition in `finishWithdrawal`, the function allows the withdrawal to be finished without enforcing the minimum withdrawal delay.
5. The user successfully withdraws the funds without waiting for the intended delay period.

References:
- [NativeVault.sol:228-294](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L228-L294)

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Update the condition in `finishWithdrawal` to check if the minimum withdrawal delay has passed

```diff
- if (startedWithdrawal.start + Constants.MIN_WITHDRAWAL_DELAY > block.timestamp) {
+ if (block.timestamp < startedWithdrawal.start + Constants.MIN_WITHDRAWAL_DELAY) {
    revert MinWithdrawDelayNotPassed();
}
```

By changing the condition to `block.timestamp < startedWithdrawal.start + Constants.MIN_WITHDRAWAL_DELAY`, the function will revert if the current timestamp is less than the start timestamp plus the minimum withdrawal delay, effectively enforcing the intended delay period before allowing the withdrawal to be finished.


## Assessed type

Timing

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Core.sol#L97-L107


# Vulnerability details

The `registerOperatorToDSS()` function allows an operator to register with a DSS. This is intended to enable the operator to allocate a portion of the assets delegated to them by stakers, there is a potential issue in the current implementation.

The `registerOperatorToDSS()` function does not check if the operator is already registered to the given DSS before proceeding with the registration. This could allow an operator to be registered multiple times to the same DSS, which might lead to unexpected behavior or errors in the system.

The root cause is in the `registerOperatorToDSS()` function itself:
```solidity
    {
        address operator = msg.sender;
        CoreLib.Storage storage self = _self();
        if (!self.isDSSRegistered(dss)) revert DSSNotRegistered();
        self.registerOperatorToDSS(dss, operator, registrationHookData);
        emit RegisteredOperatorToDSS(operator, address(dss));
    }
```
As we can see, the function checks if the `dss` is registered using `self.isDSSRegistered(dss)`, but it does not verify if the `operator` is already registered to that specific `dss`.

## Impact
If an operator can register multiple times to the same DSS, it could lead to:

   1. Incorrect accounting of the assets allocated by the operator to the DSS.
   2. exploitation of any rewards or benefits associated with the registration process.
   3. Inconsistencies in the system's state and unexpected behavior in other functions that rely on the registration status.

## Proof of Concept
The contract's behavior deviates from the expected outcome.

1. Assume that an operator, Alice, is already registered to a DSS called "StakingService".
2. Alice calls the `registerOperatorToDSS()` function again, providing the same "StakingService" DSS and some `registrationHookData`.
3. Since there is no check for the existing registration, the `self.registerOperatorToDSS()` function is called, and Alice is registered again to "StakingService".
4. This duplicate registration might cause issues in other parts of the system that assume a one-to-one relationship between operators and DSSs.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
ensure that the operator is not already registered to the given DSS. This can be done by introducing a new function in `CoreLib` to check the registration status of an operator for a specific `DSS`, and then using this function in the `registerOperatorToDSS()` function.
```diff
+ if (self.isOperatorRegisteredToDSS(operator, dss)) revert OperatorAlreadyRegistered(); self.registerOperatorToDSS(dss, operator, registrationHookData);
```


## Assessed type

Access Control

This could result in operators being incorrectly registered or failing to register when they should be able to.

## Impact

The incorrect handling of edge cases in the `registerOperatorToDSS()` function could lead to:

1. Operators being unable to register with certain DSS instances when they should be allowed to.
2. Inconsistent state between the Core contract and the DSS regarding operator registration.
3. Potential loss of functionality for affected operators, as they may be unable to allocate assets or participate in the protocol as intended.

These issues could undermine the reliability and functionality of the operator registration process, potentially affecting the overall stability and trustworthiness of the protocol.

## Proof of Concept

The function should include a check to prevent an operator from registering with a DSS they are already registered with, ensuring the integrity of the registration process.

1. An operator attempts to register with a DSS using `registerOperatorToDSS()`.
2. The function checks if the DSS is registered using `self.isDSSRegistered(dss)`.
3. Due to the edge case not being properly handled, the function fails to register the operator or registers them incorrectly.
4. The operator is now in an inconsistent state, unable to properly interact with the DSS or allocate assets.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
```solidity
function registerOperatorToDSS(IDSS dss, bytes memory registrationHookData)
    external
    whenFunctionNotPaused(Constants.PAUSE_CORE_REGISTER_TO_DSS)
    nonReentrant
{
    address operator = msg.sender;
    CoreLib.Storage storage self = _self();
    if (!self.isDSSRegistered(dss)) revert DSSNotRegistered();
    
    // Add additional checks here
    if (self.isOperatorRegisteredToDSS(operator, dss)) revert OperatorAlreadyRegistered();
    
    // Proceed with registration
    self.registerOperatorToDSS(dss, operator, registrationHookData);
    emit RegisteredOperatorToDSS(operator, address(dss));
}
```

Error

The current implementation fails to properly enforce the pause mechanism, potentially allowing unauthorized registrations during critical periods when the function should be inaccessible.

## Impact
1. Unauthorized operator registrations during emergency situations or maintenance periods.
2. Undermining of the contract's security measures and administrative controls.
3. Disruption of the protocol's intended operational flow and security assumptions.

2. Despite the pause, an operator calls the `registerOperatorToDSS()` function.
3. The function executes successfully, allowing the operator to register with a DSS.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/Core.sol#L220-#L231


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details

`Vault#deposit()` and `Vault#mint()` functions do not work well with fee-on-transfer tokens as the `assets` variable is the pre-fee amount, including the fee, whereas the `totalAssets` do not include the fee anymore.

This can be abused to mint more shares than desired.

    function deposit(uint256 assets, address to)
        public
        override(ERC4626, IVault)
        whenFunctionNotPaused(Constants.PAUSE_VAULT_DEPOSIT)
        nonReentrant
        returns (uint256 shares)
    {
        if (assets == 0) revert ZeroAmount();
        return super.deposit(assets, to);
    }

    function mint(uint256 shares, address to)
        public
        override(ERC4626, IVault)
        whenFunctionNotPaused(Constants.PAUSE_VAULT_MINT)
        nonReentrant
        returns (uint256 assets)
    {
        if (shares == 0) revert ZeroShares();
        assets = super.mint(shares, to);
    }

Example:
A `deposit(1000)` should result in the same shares as two deposits of `deposit(500)` but it does not because amount is the pre-fee amount. Assume a fee-on-transfer of 20%. Assume current `totalAmount = 1000`, `totalShares = 1000` for simplicity.

 - `deposit(1000) = 1000 / totalAmount * totalShares = 1000 shares`
 - `deposit(500) = 500 / totalAmount * totalShares = 500 shares`. Now the `totalShares` increased by `500` but the `totalAssets` only increased by `(100% - 20%) * 500 = 400`. Therefore, the second `deposit(500) = 500 / (totalAmount + 400) * (newTotalShares) = 500 / (1400) * 1500 = 535.714285714` shares.

In total, the two deposits lead to `35` more shares than a single deposit of the sum of the deposits.

## Impact
More shares can be minted.

## Tools Used
Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Shares should be minted based on the amount excluding the fee, which can be calculated by using pre-and-post balance check.





## Assessed type

Context

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/HookLib.sol#L97-L100


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

`DSS`s must conform to ERC165 interface call and in doing so enables hooks that are used by the karak protocol for various operations.

By reverting on ERC165 operations a DSS can prevent karak protocol operations like slashing, operator removal, or vault validation from working even when karak protocol could safely ignore this hooks reverting. 


## Proof of Concept

The function `callHookIfInterfaceImplemented` should not revert when `ignoreFailure` is passed as true.
But on the following line a DSS can make a non reverting call revert (as `InterfaceNotSupported()`) by removing the supported of the ERC165 interface during a hook call.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/HookLib.sol#L97-L100

This can affect operation when involving slashing:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/SlasherLib.sol#L94

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/SlasherLib.sol#L126

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/SlasherLib.sol#L153

or when unregister operator from a DSS is called:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/Operator.sol#L181

and when updating or validating vault stakes:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/Operator.sol#L61

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/Operator.sol#L111

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

When `ignoreFailure` is set to true do not revert in case of a ERC165 error:

```diff
    function callHookIfInterfaceImplemented(
        IERC165 dss,
        bytes memory data,
        bytes4 interfaceId,
        bool ignoreFailure,
        uint32 hookCallGasLimit,
        uint32 supportsInterfaceGasLimit,
        uint32 hookGasBuffer
    ) internal returns (bool) {
        ...

-        if (!success || result == bytes32(0)) {
+        if (!ignoreFailure && (!success || result == bytes32(0))) {
            // Either call failed or interface isn't implemented
            emit InterfaceNotSupported();
            return false;
        }
        ...
    }
}
```


## Assessed type

Error

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

`Core::finalizeUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` doesn't check if the operator is registered with the DSS, which allows any address to call this function and finalize stake updates.

Operator could:

1. Call `Core::requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS`
2. Unregister from the DSS by using `Core::unregisterOperatorFromDSS()`
3. Finally call `Core::finalizeUpdateStakeInDSS()`

As suggested by Renascence's audit report on the Core contract, this vulnerability could be used to:

1. Finalize stake updates for operators who are no longer registered with a DSS.
2. Bypass the intended access control, potentially leading to unauthorized stake manipulations.
3. Cause inconsistencies between the Core contract's state and the DSS's expectations, e.g. disallow DSS to slash the misbehaving operator.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Add the `checkIfOperatorIsRegInRegDSS` function call to the `Core::finalizeUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` function, to ensure only the registered operator can call the function:

```diff
function finalizeUpdateVaultStakeInDSS(Operator.QueuedStakeUpdate memory queuedStake)
    external
    nonReentrant
    whenFunctionNotPaused(Constants.PAUSE_CORE_FINALIZE_STAKE_UPDATE)
{
+   _self().checkIfOperatorIsRegInRegDSS(queuedStake.operator, queuedStake.updateRequest.dss);
    _self().validateAndUpdateVaultStakeInDSS(queuedStake);
    emit FinishedStakeUpdate(queuedStake);
}
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `Core` contract inherits from `Pauser` for its pausable functionalities. It is reasonable to assume that all DSS and operator-facing functions are intended to be pausable. However, unlike other such functions, `registerDSS()` is not modified by `whenFunctionNotPaused()` and is not pausable.

The impact of this issue is that if critical vulnerabilities are later found in the `registerDSS()` function, the manager may not be able to pause it in a timely manner.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Define a pausing index in the `Constants.sol`:
```solidity
uint8 internal constant PAUSE_CORE_REGISTER_DSS = 10;
```

Then add the `whenFunctionNotPaused` modifier to the `registerDSS()` function:
```diff
function registerDSS(uint256 maxSlashablePercentageWad) external
+ whenFunctionNotPaused(Constants.PAUSE_CORE_REGISTER_DSS)
{
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/SlashingHandler.sol#L52-L59


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
```solidity
    function handleSlashing(IERC20 token, uint256 amount) external {
        if (amount == 0) revert ZeroAmount();
        if (!_config().supportedAssets[token]) revert UnsupportedAsset();

        SafeTransferLib.safeTransferFrom(address(token), msg.sender, address(this), amount);
        // Below is where custom logic for each asset lives
        SafeTransferLib.safeTransfer(address(token), address(0), amount);
    }
```

The `handleSlashing()` function in the `SlashingHandler` contract employs a two-step transfer process:
1. It transfers the `amount` of tokens from `msg.sender` to the current contract.
2. It then transfers these tokens to `address(0)`.

If the `token` is a fee-on-transfer token, after step (1), the balance in `address(this)` will be less than `amount`, causing step (2) to fail.

Consequently, the DSS might not be able to finalize a slashing if the underlying asset in the vault is a fee-on-transfer token.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Either:
1. Do not allowlist fee-on-transfer tokens, or
2. Implement a compatible version of `SlashingHandler` for fee-on-transfer tokens.


## Assessed type

ERC20

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Vault.sol#L78


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `Vault` inherits solady's `ERC4626` implementation, which is not compatible with fee-on-transfer tokens.

`Vault`'s `deposit()` and `mint()` functions do not work well with fee-on-transfer tokens as the `amount` variable is the pre-fee amount, including the fee, whereas the `totalAssets` do not include the fee anymore.

This can be abused to mint more shares than desired:

A deposit(1000) should result in the same shares as two deposits of deposit(500) but it does not because amount is the pre-fee amount. Assume a fee-on-transfer of 20%, and ignore the virtual share in ERC4626 for simplicity. Assume current totalAmount = 1000, totalShares = 1000.

- `deposit(1000) = 1000 / totalAmount * totalShares = 1000 shares`
- `deposit(500) = 500 / totalAmount * totalShares = 500 shares`. Now the totalShares increased by 500 but the totalAssets only increased by (100% - 20%) * 500 = 400. Therefore, the second deposit(500) = 500 / (totalAmount + 400) * (newTotalShares) = 500 / (1400) * 1500 = 535.714285714 shares.

In total, the two deposits lead to 35 more shares than a single deposit of the sum of the deposits.



## Tools Used
Mannual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
`amount` should be the amount excluding the fee. Consider override `previewDeposit` and `previewMint` to support fee-on-transfer tokens.


## Assessed type

ERC20

the snapshot function is used by a nativenodeowner to keep the NativeNode aware of the balance changes on the beacon chain. if (validatorDetails.lastBalanceUpdateTimestamp >= node.currentSnapshotTimestamp) {

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
If address(0) is passed the function will not revert as it was intended to do because of a mistake in the check.

## Proof of Concept
Currently this is how we check if the code should revert or not:
```diff
if (!(implementation == address(0) || isVaultImplAllowlisted(self, implementation))) {
            revert VaultImplNotAllowlisted();
}
```
 however if address(0) is passed this check will fail to revert, because the current logic will look like this: !(true || false) which evaluates to !true and results to false, so we will not enter the if body.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider changing the following:
```diff
-   if (!(implementation == address(0) || isVaultImplAllowlisted(self, implementation))) {
+   if (implementation == address(0) || !isVaultImplAllowlisted(self, implementation)) {
            revert VaultImplNotAllowlisted();
}
```

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/a9658bccc884eb72538875c3940c6b507e06d4ca/src/Core.sol#L248


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
A malicious `Operator` would not get the slashing penalty when they behave maliciously towards a `DSS` 

## Proof of Concept
A `vault` is usually staked to any `DSS` of the `Operator's` choice and can be staked to a max of `32 DSS`. Staking a `vault` to a large number of `DSS's` (maybe 15, 16, 19, 24 or more) could be seen as "Overleveraging". 
   These `DSS's` have a slashable percentage in the event of an `Operator` operating maliciously. The `DSS` can jail a certain vault for overleveraging. As the docs mentioned:
> The effects of jailing are arbitrary and can be decided by the `DSS`. 
  This can range from no rewards to not allowing the operator to perform any tasks and forcing them to unallocate from the DSS.

The issue here is that a `vault` might not necessarily be overleveraging but can be registered to only 3-4 `DSS's` that have a high slashing percentage. By just checking for the max `DSS` registered to a vault, it won't be seen as "Overleveraging" and in the case where the `Operator` performs malicously across the `DSS's` and tries to be slashed atleast one or two `DSS` will lose out thereby leaving the malicious `Operator` unslashed. 
From the code we can see that the 
```solidity
`MAX_SLASHING_PERCENT_WAD = HUNDRED_PERCENT_WAD`
```
 Meaning that a `DSS` can set a slashing percentage of up to a 100%.
Lets say a `Vault` is registered to 4 `DSS's` with about 35% slashing percentage each, in the event of malicious activity by the `Operator`, all of them can't and won't be able to slash the Vault as at least one or two will loose out and this violates the intended design on what and how slashing should work.  

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Asides from checking if a vault is "overleveraged", it should be able to check or oversee the slashing percentage a couple of DSS's registered to a vault have so as to prevent this type of occurences.





## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/Operator.sol#L123-L133


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The `msg.sender` might get potential rewards instead of the operator.

## Proof of Concept

This issue is not mitigated yet from a past report. High severity is set as per the past report, but I believe Medium severity to be more accurate.

In the IDSS interface, the parameter of `finishUpdateStakeHook()` is `operator`.

```
    function finishUpdateStakeHook(address operator) external;
```

However, in `validateAndUpdateVaultStakeInDSS()`, the forwarded parameter is `msg.sender`.

```
  IDSS dss = queuedStakeUpdate.updateRequest.dss;
        HookLib.callHookIfInterfaceImplemented({
            dss: dss,
>           data: abi.encodeWithSelector(dss.finishUpdateStakeHook.selector, msg.sender),
            interfaceId: dss.finishUpdateStakeHook.selector,
            ignoreFailure: true,
            hookCallGasLimit: self.hookCallGasLimit,
            supportsInterfaceGasLimit: self.supportsInterfaceGasLimit,
            hookGasBuffer: self.hookGasBuffer
        });
```

Since anyone can call `finalizeUpdateVaultStakeInDSS()` in Core.sol, this causes the caller address to be treated as the operator in DSS’s `finishUpdateStakeHook()` to execute the associated logic, which could involve something like registering the address to receive rewards.

```
    function finalizeUpdateVaultStakeInDSS(Operator.QueuedStakeUpdate memory queuedStake)
        external
        nonReentrant
        whenFunctionNotPaused(Constants.PAUSE_CORE_FINALIZE_STAKE_UPDATE)
    {
>       _self().validateAndUpdateVaultStakeInDSS(queuedStake);
        emit FinishedStakeUpdate(queuedStake);
    }
```


[Past report link](https://code4rena.com/reports/2024-06-karak-pro-league#h-03-validateandupdatevaultstakeindss-forwards-incorrect-operator-address-to-finishupdatestakehook)

## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Use the `operator` like how it is done in other hooks:

```
 HookLib.callHookIfInterfaceImplemented({
            dss: dss,
>           data: abi.encodeWithSelector(dss.unregistrationHook.selector, operator, unregistrationHookData),
            interfaceId: dss.unregistrationHook.selector,
            ignoreFailure: true, // So it can't prevent the operator from unregistering
            hookCallGasLimit: self.hookCallGasLimit,
            supportsInterfaceGasLimit: self.supportsInterfaceGasLimit,
            hookGasBuffer: self.hookGasBuffer
        });
```

Context

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Core.sol#L85


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

All assets which are meant to be slashed by DSS can be misused by the rogue or compromised Manager. In addition, attacker which has previously compromised Manager EOA and has this capability can use intentionally to break security rules/invariants of particular DSS. 

## Proof of Concept

In [SlasherLib.finalizeSlashing()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/SlasherLib.sol#L135..L138) slashingHandler for particular asset is dynamically retrieved and passed to [Vault.slashAssets()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Vault.sol#L193..L205) function. Vault fully trusts provided slashingHandler contract and approves for transfer designated amount meant to be slashed.

However, account with Manager role, which can be EOA as stated by the client, may change at any point slashingHandler for any asset through Core.allowlistAssets() and CoreLib.allowlistAssets(). As a result, compromised Manager EOA may update trusted slashingHandler implementation for popular asset with contract which would drain and redirect assets meant to be slashed. In addition, attacker (compromised manager) may trigger this operation by directly calling Core.finalizeSlashing()

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

- Do not allow slashing handler to be changed, or enforce timelocked updates for any slashing handler change.


## Assessed type

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L448


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`node.withdrawableCreditedNodeETH` = the amount of ETH ever held by the native node as it is increased in `_updateSnapshot()` by `nodeBalanceWei`:
```solidity
node.withdrawableCreditedNodeETH += snapshot.nodeBalanceWei;
```
Note that `node.withdrawableCreditedNodeETH` is not modified anywhere else in the code. `node.withdrawableCreditedNodeETH` is used in `_startSnapshot()` to calculate the amount of ETH gained by the native node since the last snapshot:
```solidity
// Calculate unattributed node balance
uint256 nodeBalanceWei = node.nodeAddress.balance - node.withdrawableCreditedNodeETH;
```
The native node's ETH balance will become smaller than `node.withdrawableCreditedNodeETH`. Thus, when `_startSnapshot()` is called, `node.nodeAddress.balance` - `node.withdrawableCreditedNodeETH` will revert.
## Proof Of Concept
1. Alice's native node has 5 ETH of balance. (`nodeAddress.balance` && `node.withdrawableCreditedNodeETH` = 5e18)
2. Alice withdraws 1 ETH from the native node.
3. After that, `_startSnapshot()` is called
4. `nodeAddress.balance` - `node.withdrawableCreditedNodeETH` = 4e18 - 5e18 (reverts)
## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
`node.withdrawableCreditedNodeETH` should store the balance of the native node during the last snapshot


## Assessed type

Under/Overflow

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/ab18e1f6c03e118158369527baa2487b2b4616b1/src/entities/SlasherLib.sol#L94-L124

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/ab18e1f6c03e118158369527baa2487b2b4616b1/src/Vault.sol#L125-L149
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/ab18e1f6c03e118158369527baa2487b2b4616b1/src/Vault.sol#L157-L188


# Vulnerability details

The vulnerability stems from a timing issue in the slashing mechanism, where the amount to be slashed is calculated at the time of request but not updated at the time of finalization. This can lead to inconsistencies in the slashed amounts due to changes in the vault's total assets during the delay period.

### Vulnerable Process Flow

1. **Slashing Request:**
   - `earmarkedStakes` are calculated based on the current `totalAssets()` of each vault.
   - These values are stored in the `QueuedSlashing` struct.

2. **Time Delay:**
   - A minimum delay of `Constants.SLASHING_VETO_WINDOW` exists between request and finalization.
   - During this period, vault assets can change due to:
     - Deposits (`deposit` function)
     - Mints (`mint` function)
     - Withdrawals (`startRedeem` and `finishRedeem` functions)

3. **Slashing Finalization:**
   - The pre-calculated `earmarkedStakes` are used without rechecking the current `totalAssets()`.

### Potential Impacts

1. **If total assets increase:**
   - The slashed amount will be less than intended as a percentage of current assets.
   - This could lead to under-punishing of malicious actors.

2. **If total assets decrease:**
   - The slashed amount could be a higher percentage than initially intended.
   - While `Math.min()` in `slashAssets` prevents slashing more than available, it could still result in over-punishing.

### Root Cause

The core issue is that the slashed amount doesn't accurately reflect the intended percentage of the vault's assets at the time of slashing execution. This discrepancy arises from the time delay between calculation and execution, during which the vault's total assets can change.

### Recommendation

To address this vulnerability, consider implementing one of the following solutions:

1. Recalculate the slash amount during finalization based on:
   - The current `totalAssets()`
   - The originally requested slash percentage

2. Implement a mechanism to freeze deposits and withdrawals for the affected vault once a slash is requested, until it's either finalized or cancelled.

These changes would ensure that the slashed amount accurately reflects the intended percentage of the current vault assets.





## Assessed type

Timing

# Vulnerability details

Centralization Risk for trusted owners

Contracts have owners with privileged rights to perform admin tasks and need to be trusted to not perform malicious updates or drain funds


Key Points of the Vulnerability
Privileged Rights: The owner or administrator has special rights that ordinary users do not possess. These rights are necessary for maintaining and managing the contract but also pose a risk if not handled correctly.

Trust Requirement: Users of the contract must trust the owner to act in their best interests and not abuse their privileges. If the owner is malicious or becomes compromised, they could perform harmful actions, such as:

Draining funds from the contract.
Deploying malicious updates.
Changing important configurations to benefit themselves.
Centralized Control: This ownership model introduces a level of centralization to an otherwise decentralized system. While this is sometimes necessary for practical purposes, it contradicts the ethos of decentralization and can be a single point of failure.


- Found in src/SlashingHandler.sol [Line: 16](src/SlashingHandler.sol#L16)

- Found in src/SlashingHandler.sol [Line: 43](src/SlashingHandler.sol#L43)

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/Core.sol#L151
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/entities/Operator.sol#L126


# Vulnerability details

## Details
- The `finalizeUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` function calls the `validateAndUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` function to perform the updations related to finalize the staking of the vault to the DSS and it calls the hook function `finishUpdateStakeHook` on DSS.
- The `finishUpdateStakeHook` function takes in operator as parameter and `msg.sender` is passed to it considering that only operator would call it.
- But as the `finalizeUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` function is allowed to be called by anyone, therefore it would result in passing incorrect operator to the DSS via the `finishUpdateStakeHook` function as it passes the `msg.sender` which would not be the operator in case anyone other than actual operator calls it.

## Impact
Incorrect data is sent to DSS through the `finishUpdateStakeHook` function as `msg.sender` will not always the operator which would result in incorrect accounting on the operator and even result in severe destruction of the DSS.


## Proof of Concept
- As the `finalizeUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` function can be called by anyone, therefore `msg.sender` will not always be the operator.
```solidity
    function validateAndUpdateVaultStakeInDSS(CoreLib.Storage storage self, QueuedStakeUpdate memory queuedStakeUpdate)
        external
    {
        State storage operatorState = self.operatorState[queuedStakeUpdate.operator];
        validateQueuedStakeUpdate(operatorState, queuedStakeUpdate);
        updateVaultStakeInDSS(
            operatorState,
            queuedStakeUpdate.updateRequest.vault,
            queuedStakeUpdate.updateRequest.dss,
            queuedStakeUpdate.updateRequest.toStake
        );
        delete operatorState.pendingStakeUpdates[queuedStakeUpdate.updateRequest.vault];
        IDSS dss = queuedStakeUpdate.updateRequest.dss;
        HookLib.callHookIfInterfaceImplemented({
            dss: dss,
@>          data: abi.encodeWithSelector(dss.finishUpdateStakeHook.selector, msg.sender),
            interfaceId: dss.finishUpdateStakeHook.selector,
            ignoreFailure: true,
            hookCallGasLimit: self.hookCallGasLimit,
            supportsInterfaceGasLimit: self.supportsInterfaceGasLimit,
            hookGasBuffer: self.hookGasBuffer
        });
    }
``` 

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Either make the `finalizeUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` function to be called only by respective operator who created a request related to the updation of their vaults or replace msg.sender by the actual operator, i.e. `queuedStakeUpdate.operator`.


## Assessed type

Context

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/SlashingHandler.sol#L53


# Vulnerability details

## Details
- The finalize slashing involves slashing of a certain number of vaults of the operator by the DSS.
- The `SlasherLib::finalizeSlashing` involves calling the `slashAssets` for every vault which in turn calls the `handleSlashing` function on the `SlashingHandler`.
- The vulnerability occurs when for a vault for which the slashing amount becomes `0` will lead to DoS, thus failing the whole txn and DSS would not be able to perform the slashing, while the operator would be able to withdraw all their stakes as time would be passed till then.


## Proof of Concept
The reason behind slashing amount becoming 0 can be due to the following cases:

1. Case I
- The malicious operator has their own malicious DSS (having max slashable percentage set to 100%) which either front-runs the genuine DSS slashing request or is active enough to perform their own slashing before in time for their vault and performs it only for a single vault that they can sacrifice and is also contained in the genuine DSS slashing.
- As well as the malicious operator also places the vault unstake request before the above step.
- Then, the malicious operator would be able to finalize their own slashing request first as it was placed before in time, leading to amount to be reduced to 0 on a vault, and then when the genuine DSS tries to finalize their slashing request it would revert their whole txn as for a vault the amount was reduced to 0 (sacrificed by the operator to be able to unstake their other vaults).
- Finally the operator unstakes all of their vaults.

   

2. Case II
- The other case would be that the operator have leveraged their vault to multiple DSS, and this time consider the malicious DSS `B` to be a genuine DSS with same max slashing percentage set to 100%.
- Consider the case that they have stakes multiple vaults to DSS A, and single vault to DSS B, and that single vault is also in DSS A, and now both DSSs detects the malicious behavior of operator and they passes all the respective staked vault for slashing, and consider that the DSS B's finalize slashing happens before DSS A, resulting in failure of DSS A slashing due to a revert due to `0` amount of a particular vault.
- And the DSS would be able to unstake their vaults (note: they placed their unstake request as soon as they saw the slashing request).


## Impact
DSS would face a DoS due to the revert in `handleSlashing` for the amount being 0 for the case discussed in this finding and thus would not be able to slash the operator, thus giving the operator the opportunity to unstake their vaults.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Remove the revert condition in `SlashingHandler::handleSlashing` where it reverts for the case when amount is 0.


## Assessed type

DoS

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/Core.sol#L146


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
- The `finalizeUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` function allows the operators to still register to the DSS even after unregistering from them after placing the vault stake update request.
- This allows them to prevent from getting slashed from the operators and perform their tasks.

## Proof of Concept
```solidity
    function finalizeUpdateVaultStakeInDSS(Operator.QueuedStakeUpdate memory queuedStake)
        external
        nonReentrant
        whenFunctionNotPaused(Constants.PAUSE_CORE_FINALIZE_STAKE_UPDATE)
    {
        _self().validateAndUpdateVaultStakeInDSS(queuedStake);
        emit FinishedStakeUpdate(queuedStake);
    }
```

- Operator registers them to a DSS.
- Then deploys their vault and creates a request to register on DSS.
- Then unregisters from DSS, the operator will be able to perform this task as they have no vault staked to that DSS (only request is placed, but to the mapping corresponding to that DSS no vaults are added in the array).
- Then call the `finalizeUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` to finally update their stake to the DSS.
- Thus, operator have successfully put their stake to DSS, but are actually not registered.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
In the `finalizeUpdateVaultStakeInDSS`, add the following function check:
```solidity
isOperatorRegisteredToDSS(queuedStake.operator, queuedStake.updateRequest.dss)
```


## Assessed type

Context

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L308


# Vulnerability details

## Bug description
When assets are allowlisted in the Core, it's assigned a slashingHandler.

[CoreLib.sol#L73](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/CoreLib.sol#L73)
```solidity
self.assetSlashingHandlers[assets[i]] = slashingHandlers[i];
```

When NativeVault is being initialized, the slashStore is stored in storage.

[NativeVault.sol#L75](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L75)
```solidity
self.slashStore = slashStore;
```
When slashing is being finalized, `Vault.slashAssets()` is called with slashingHandler as one of the parameters. More specifically, the parameter is retrieved from the `assetSlashingHandlers` mapping of the Core contract.

[SlasherLib.sol#L135-L138](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/SlasherLib.sol#L135-L138)
```solidity
IKarakBaseVault(queuedSlashing.vaults[i]).slashAssets(
    queuedSlashing.earmarkedStakes[i],
    self.assetSlashingHandlers[
        IKarakBaseVault(queuedSlashing.vaults[i]).asset()
    ]
);
```

In the `NativeVault::slashAssets()` exists a check that ensures that `slashStore` of the NativeVault is equal to the `slashingHandler` of the underlying asset.

[NativeVault.sol#L308](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L308)
```solidity
if (slashingHandler != self.slashStore) revert NotSlashStore();
```

If after a vault was deployed with the correct slashStore, the slashingHandler is changed for ETH as an underlying asset, the slashing won't work for such vaults. 

## Impact
DoS of slashing.


## Recommended Mitigation
Allow the manager to change the slashStore of the NativeVault.


## Assessed type

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/Operator.sol#L126


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
DSS will receive incorrect operator address in `dss.finishUpdateStakeHook()` hook.

## Proof of Concept

After a stake vault update request is made, the `Core::finalizeUpdateVaultStakeInDSS()` function must be called to finalize the request, and the protocol allows anyone to call this function.

So in the function calling, `msg.sender` may or may not be an operator. When calling `HookLib.callHookIfInterfaceImplemented()` in the `validateAndUpdateVaultStakeInDSS()` function, `msg.sender` is passed along with `dss.finishUpdateStakeHook.selector`.

```solidity
    function validateAndUpdateVaultStakeInDSS(CoreLib.Storage storage self, QueuedStakeUpdate memory queuedStakeUpdate)
        external
    {
        ... ...
        HookLib.callHookIfInterfaceImplemented({
            dss: dss,
            data: abi.encodeWithSelector(dss.finishUpdateStakeHook.selector, msg.sender), // @audit --> `msg.sender` is passed
            interfaceId: dss.finishUpdateStakeHook.selector,
            ignoreFailure: true,
            hookCallGasLimit: self.hookCallGasLimit,
            supportsInterfaceGasLimit: self.supportsInterfaceGasLimit,
            hookGasBuffer: self.hookGasBuffer
        });
    }
```

Therefore, the DSS may receive an incorrect address as an operator (or potentially a malicious hacker) and proceed with further operations using this address.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Just pass `queuedStakeUpdate.operator` instead of `msg.sender`.



## Assessed type

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/entities/CoreLib.sol#L132-L145
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/NativeVault.sol#L83-L92


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Malicious operators may deploy the native vaults with their own native node implementation addresses. With these customized native nodes, they can run bad actions, such as stealing node owners' withdrawn ETHs that must be sent to the owners' intended addresses.

## Proof of Concept

When creating a native vault, the implementation address of Native Node is provided through the `extraData` parameter.

Neither `CoreLib::deployVaults()` nor `CoreLib::createVault()` conduct a whitelist validation of the native node implementation, and any contract can be a logic contract address of the deployed native node proxy.

As being an operator doesn't require owner's approval, anybody can be an operator without any problem.

Consequently, a malicious operator may create a native vault with a bad native node implementation. Or after creating a vault with a normal node implementation, he may change it to malicious code later through the `NativeVault::changeNodeImplementation()` function.

### PoC Test

To prove this, I modified the `nativeVault.t.sol` by changing line 85 from
```solidity
    address nativeNodeImpl = address(new NativeNode());
```
to
```solidity
    address nativeNodeImpl = address(0xdeadbeaf);
```

And added the below new test case:
```solidity
    function test_createNode_badImpl(address nodeOwner) public {
        assertEq(nativeVault.implementation(), address(0xdeadbeef));
    }

```

Here's logs of successful running of the test case:
```
Ran 1 test for test/nativeRestaking/nativeVault.t.sol:NativeVaultTest
[PASS] test_createNode_badImpl(address) (runs: 257, μ: 32567, ~: 32567)
Suite result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 skipped; finished in 14.13ms (10.92ms CPU time)
```


## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider implementing an allowlist for native node implementations, similar to the vault implementation allowlist, to be managed under the Core owner's authority. And then add performing whiteness validation check of `implementation` from `extraData` parameter in `CoreLib::deployVaults()` or `CoreLib::createVault()` functions.

This allowlist check should also be conducted for `NativeVault::changeNodeImplementation()` function.
















## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/Vault.sol#L78-L87
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/Vault.sol#L94-L103
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/Vault.sol#L110-L119


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Karak uses an implementation of the ERC4626 tokenized vault standard as the default vault to handle ERC20 tokens as restaked assets. Each asset has a dedicated vault.
However, the ERC4626 `deposit/mint` functions do not work well with fee-on-transfer tokens. The `amount` variable represents the pre-fee amount, including the fee, whereas the `totalAssets` no longer include the fee.

Vaults that handle tokens with fee-on-transfer can be exploited to mint more shares than intended.
```solidity
File:ERC4626.sol
function _deposit(address by, address to, uint256 assets, uint256 shares) internal virtual {
    SafeTransferLib.safeTransferFrom(asset(), by, address(this), assets);
    _mint(to, shares);
    /// @solidity memory-safe-assembly
    assembly {
        // Emit the {Deposit} event.
        mstore(0x00, assets)
        mstore(0x20, shares)
        let m := shr(96, not(0))
        log3(0x00, 0x40, _DEPOSIT_EVENT_SIGNATURE, and(m, by), and(m, to))
    }
    _afterDeposit(assets, shares);
}
```
At the same time, users that mint directly the assets using `mint()` function in `Vault.sol` will be disadvantage, receiving fewer assets than intended.

## Proof of Concept
A `deposit(1000)` should result in the same number of shares as two deposits of `deposit(500)` but it does not because `amount` is the pre-fee amount.
Assume a fee-on-transfer of `20%`. For simplicity, let's assume the current `totalAmount = 1000` and `totalShares = 1000`.

- `deposit(1000) = 1000 / totalAmount * totalShares = 1000 shares`
- `deposit(500) = 500 / totalAmount * totalShares = 500 shares`. Now the `totalShares` increased by 500, but the `totalAssets` only increased by `(100% - 20%) * 500 = 400`. Therefore, the second `deposit(500) = 500 / (totalAmount + 400) * (newTotalShares) = 500 / (1400) * 1500 = 535.714285714 shares`.

In total, the two deposits result in `35` more shares than a single deposit of the sum of the deposits.

## Tools Used
Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
`amount` should be the amount excluding the fee, i.e., the amount the contract actually received. This can be achieved by subtracting the pre-contract balance from the post-contract balance.

Additioally, `previewDeposit` should be overwritten by vaults supporting fee-on-transfer tokens to predict the post-fee `amount` and perform the shares computation based on that amount. However, `afterDeposit` will still be called with the original `amount`, and implementers need to be aware of this.


## Assessed type

ERC4626

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/NativeVaultLib.sol#L127-L132


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Validators are able to completely avoid DSS slash events by withdrawing their entire stake on the Beacon Chain right before the slashing occurs, causing a loss of funds for the protocol.

## Proof of Concept
Here, I will explain why the attack is possible and how it can be performed:
For simplicity, we will assume that the validator, escaping the slash event, has a `NativeNode` with a balance of 0 and a stake on the Beacon Chain of 32 ETH, therefore their `snapshot.nodeBalanceWei = 0` and `ownerToNode[validator].totalRestakedETH = 32 ETH`.

The validator notices that a slash event will occur soon, the slashing is intended to reduce the `totalAssets` by 50%. In order to not suffer any losses the malicious validator calls `startSnapshot`, if needed, and after that exits their position on the Beacon Chain, withdrawing the 32 ETH of stake to their native node.

The withdrawn 32 ETH is yet to be recorded and `snapshot.nodeBalanceWei` is still 0. Now the validator makes a call to `validateSnapshotProofs`. As the validator has exited their stake, `balanceDeltaWei` will be -32 ETH and `_updateSnapshot` will burn the entirety of the validator's shares, also reducing their `totalRestakedETH` to 0. Therefore, the validator currently has a node with `snapshot.nodeBalanceWei = 0`, while in reality there are 32 ETH in the native node contract.

Now after the slashing occurs and `totalAssets` are reduced, the validator calls `startSnapshot`, which does not transfer any funds to the slash store as `totalRestakedETH` would still be 0. Furthermore, the function increases their `snapshot.nodeBalanceWei` to 32 ETH, allowing them to withdraw their funds without any harm from the slash events.

It is important to note that even if the DSS notices this malicious behaviour and performs another slash, other validators will be harmed and lose funds from the actions of the attacker.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
In `validateSnapshotProofs` update appropriately the validator's node `snapshot.nodeBalanceWei` if funds have been withdrawn from the Beacon Chain to the native node.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L83-L92


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`NativeVault.sol`'s `changeNodeImplementation` function can only be called by the `Core` contract or the `MANAGER_ROLE`. As this function is never called in the `Core` contract, practically only the manager of the Native Vault can call it. 

As a result, through the `changeNodeImplementation` function malicious Native Vault managers can steal all funds from users' nodes or may prevent vaults from being slashed.

It is important to note that even though Native Vault managers are granted a role with the same name as the trusted Core manager's role, the two roles are completely different, as the Native Vault manager's role is granted by untrusted addresses.

The issue is that the manager is specified by the operator of the Native Vault. As operators are not trusted, Native Vault managers can also not be trusted and may be malicious contracts.

## Proof of Concept
As we can see `changeNodeImplementation` allows the untrusted manager to change the implementation contract of the Native node:
```solidity
    function changeNodeImplementation(address newNodeImplementation)
        external
        onlyOwnerOrRoles(Constants.MANAGER_ROLE)
        whenFunctionNotPaused(Constants.PAUSE_NATIVEVAULT_NODE_IMPLEMENTATION)
    {
        if (newNodeImplementation == address(0)) revert ZeroAddress();

        _state().nodeImpl = newNodeImplementation;
        emit UpgradedAllNodes(newNodeImplementation);
    }
```

Therefore, any funds stored in the Native node contracts may be stolen by simply changing the implementation to a malicious contract. Furthermore, this can prevent the slash store from receiving any slashed funds.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Perhaps, Native Vault managers should be the same as the manager of the Core contract.


## Assessed type

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L181-L187


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The timestamp validation of `beaconStateRootProof.timestamp` in `validateWithdrawalCredentials` is insufficient and may cause validators to be minted more shares than intended.

## Proof of Concept
This is the validation of the `beaconStateRootProof` timestamp:
```solidity
    if (beaconStateRootProof.timestamp == block.timestamp) {
        revert BeaconTimestampIsCurrent();
    }
    if (
        beaconStateRootProof.timestamp < node.lastSnapshotTimestamp
            || beaconStateRootProof.timestamp < node.currentSnapshotTimestamp
    ) revert BeaconTimestampTooOld();
```

`beaconStateRootProof` is specified by node owners and is used to validate the provided `validatorFieldsProofs` against the beacon block root. The issue is that this validation is insufficient and may allow stale `validatorFieldsProofs` to be valid.

As we can see from EigenLayer's implementation, it is essential that the withdrawal credential proof is not stale as the validator may have been slashed in a more recent beacon state root:
https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/bb5ae1822e0444dde1fe95f45cb0d77bf0983436/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L331-L334
```solidity
/**
         * Withdrawal credential proof should not be "stale" (older than VERIFY_BALANCE_UPDATE_WINDOW_SECONDS) as we are doing a balance check here
         * The validator container persists as the state evolves and even after the validator exits. So we can use a more "fresh" credential proof within
         * the VERIFY_BALANCE_UPDATE_WINDOW_SECONDS window, not just the first proof where the validator container is registered in the state.
         */
        require(
            oracleTimestamp + VERIFY_BALANCE_UPDATE_WINDOW_SECONDS >= block.timestamp,
            "EigenPod.verifyWithdrawalCredentials: specified timestamp is too far in past"
        );
```

In the EigenLayer implementation the `oracleTimestamp` variable is the `beaconStateRootProof.timestamp`. It is validated that it is not older than `VERIFY_BALANCE_UPDATE_WINDOW_SECONDS`:
https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/bb5ae1822e0444dde1fe95f45cb0d77bf0983436/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L43-L47
```solidity
    /**
     * @notice Maximum "staleness" of a Beacon Chain state root against which `verifyBalanceUpdate` or `verifyWithdrawalCredentials` may be proven.
     * We can't allow "stale" roots to be used for restaking as the validator may have been slashed in a more updated beacon state root.
     */
    uint256 internal constant VERIFY_BALANCE_UPDATE_WINDOW_SECONDS = 4.5 hours;
```

This validation is missing in the `NativeVault.sol` contract. Furthermore, `beaconStateRootProof.timestamp` in some cases is not even validated as `node.lastSnapshotTimestamp` and `node.currentSnapshotTimestamp` can even be zero if a snapshot is yet to start.

As a result, stale roots may be used to acquire the validator's withdrawal credentials. If a slash on a validator has happened in a more recent beacon state root, the validator will receive more shares of the Native Vault than expected. With more shares, they will be gaining a higher number of rewards unfairly.

Furthermore, it is also important to be aware that in `validateSnapshotProofs` the `snapshot.parentBeaconBlockRoot` that is used to validate the `balanceContainer` may also be stale.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Include a check that `beaconStateRootProof.timestamp` is not older than `4.5 hours` in `validateWithdrawalCredentials`.


## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/HookLib.sol#L87-L89
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/HookLib.sol#L55


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In `HookLib.sol` `callHookIfInterfaceImplemented` and `callHook` validate that there is enough gas for the function call to be successful. The issue is that the functions make wrong calculations, which may cause the execution to revert even though, it would have been successful, or not revert when it should have failed. 

In the first case this may prevent users from updating their stake in DSS, initiating and finalizing slashing and configuring operators' registration to DSS. In the second case this will allow malicious operators to bypass the validation, enabling them to execute the [H-02] attack from the Karak Pro League audit: https://code4rena.com/reports/2024-06-karak-pro-league#h-02-malicious-operators-can-bypass-checks-in-dss-hooks

## Proof of Concept
The following validation is made in `callHookIfInterfaceImplemented` and `callHook`:
```solidity
if (gasleft() < (supportsInterfaceGasLimit * 64 / 63 + hookGasBuffer)) {
    revert NotEnoughGas();
}
```

Here we can see that in order for a call to be successful `gasleft` needs to be more than `(supportsInterfaceGasLimit * 64 / 63 + hookGasBuffer)`.

However, there is a mistake in the calculation, causing it to act unexpectedly. Assuming that `supportsInterfaceGasLimit + hookGasBuffer` is what the rest of the execution will consume, the needed gas will not be `(supportsInterfaceGasLimit * 64 / 63 + hookGasBuffer)`. Instead, the validation should be performed as follows:
```solidity
if (gasleft() < hookGasBuffer || (gasleft() - hookGasBuffer) * 63 / 64 < supportsInterfaceGasLimit) {
    revert NotEnoughGas();
}
```

This is the case as we are assuming that `performLowLevelCallAndLimitReturnData` will consume `hookGasBuffer`. After that in the low-level call `supportsInterfaceGasLimit` needs to be less than or equal to 63/64 of the remaining gas.

Due to the issue, the function may revert incorrectly, preventing users from interacting with the `Core` contract, or, even worse, it may not revert when intended, enabling malicious operators to bypass checks in DSS hooks.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Update the gas validation as follows:
```solidity
if (gasleft() < hookGasBuffer || (gasleft() - hookGasBuffer) / 63 * 64 < supportsInterfaceGasLimit) {
    revert NotEnoughGas();
}
```

Other
